title: Political Thought
topics: Inequalities of power in modern politics
Overlooked voices: Douglass, Cooper, Nkrumah, Davis

notes.h: Inequalities of power in modern politics
notes.body:
The central question is whether power in modern democracies is dispersed or concentrated, and how we could tell.

Definitions
- Weber: power (Macht) is the probability of carrying out one's will despite resistance; domination (Herrschaft) is the probability that commands will be obeyed, usually resting on belief in legitimacy.
- Dahl: A has power over B to the extent that A gets B to do something B would not otherwise do.
- Power-over (control of others) differs from power-to (capacity to act, often collectively). Arendt (On Violence, 1970) held that power arises when people act in concert, while violence can destroy power but never create it.

The debate
- Pluralism: Dahl's Who Governs? (1961) found different groups winning on different issues in New Haven, so power was dispersed among competing elites.
- Elite theory: C. Wright Mills (The Power Elite, 1956) described an interlocking corporate, military and political elite.
- Second face: Bachrach and Baratz (1962) argued power is also exercised through non-decision-making, keeping issues off the agenda. Schattschneider (1960) called this the 'mobilisation of bias' and said the pluralist chorus sings with an upper-class accent.
- Third dimension: Lukes (Power: A Radical View, 1974) added the shaping of wants and beliefs so that conflict never surfaces, against people's 'real interests'. Critics ask who decides those interests; Lukes appealed to what people would choose under relative autonomy.
- Structural power: Lindblom (Politics and Markets, 1977) argued business has a 'privileged position' because governments depend on investment. Gilens and Page (2014) found economic elites and business groups had substantial independent influence on US policy, average citizens little or none.
- Gramsci: ruling classes govern largely through consent, making their worldview common sense through civil society.
- Foucault (Discipline and Punish, 1975): modern power is diffuse and productive, working through surveillance and normalisation, modelled on Bentham's panopticon.

Applied example
If a council never debates rent control because councillors assume landlords would block it, Dahl's method sees no exercise of power, Bachrach and Baratz see a non-decision, and Lukes asks whether tenants have come to see high rents as natural.

Exam pitfalls
- Treating the three faces as rival definitions rather than cumulative critiques; Lukes's view includes the first two.
- Confusing unequal resources with a single ruling group: pluralists accepted the first but denied the second.
- Using Foucault without addressing the objection that if power is everywhere, domination becomes hard to tell apart from ordinary social life.
- Ignoring the measurement problem: the deeper the dimension, the harder it is to observe.

Debates about freedom ask what freedom is, and whether poverty, dependence or one's own desires can make a person unfree.

Negative and positive liberty
- Berlin, 'Two Concepts of Liberty' (1958): negative liberty is the area within which one is not interfered with by others; positive liberty is self-mastery, being governed by one's own rational will, or sharing in collective self-government.
- Berlin feared positive liberty because it splits the self into a 'true' and an empirical self, licensing coercion in the name of the first. Rousseau's citizen who is 'forced to be free' (Social Contract, 1762, I.7) is his paradigm.
- Hobbes (Leviathan, ch. 21): liberty is the absence of external impediments, and acting from fear is still free.
- The contented slave: if freedom were getting what one wants, one could become freer by giving up desires. Berlin rejected this 'retreat to the inner citadel'.

Refinements and rivals
- MacCallum (1967): every freedom claim has the form 'x is free from y to do or become z', so the two concepts are disagreements about the variables.
- Taylor (1979): opportunity versus exercise concepts; we must judge which freedoms are significant.
- Constant (1819): liberty of the ancients (participation) versus the moderns (private independence).
- Republicanism: Skinner (Liberty before Liberalism, 1998) and Pettit (Republicanism, 1997) define freedom as non-domination, not being subject to another's capacity for arbitrary interference. A slave with a kind master is unfree; non-arbitrary law need not reduce freedom.
- Mill's harm principle (On Liberty, 1859): power may be exercised over someone against their will only to prevent harm to others. He excluded children and 'barbarians'.
- G. A. Cohen: money works like a ticket; without it you will be physically stopped from boarding the train, so poverty restricts negative liberty itself.

Applied example
A zero-hours worker whose manager can cancel her shifts at will, though he never does, suffers no actual interference on a pure negative view, but is unfree on the republican view because she lives at another's mercy. Cohen would add that lacking money exposes her to interference whenever she tries to use goods she cannot pay for.

Exam pitfalls
- Equating positive liberty with having resources; for Berlin it concerns self-mastery and who governs.
- Treating republican freedom as positive liberty; Pettit presents it as a distinct third view focused on dependence.
- Stating the harm principle without its difficulties: what counts as harm, and whether offence or self-harm qualifies.
- Forgetting that Berlin himself said negative liberty is one value among many.

The core question is what, if anything, gives a state the right to rule and its citizens a duty to obey.

Definitions
- Weber ('Politics as a Vocation', 1919): the state successfully claims the monopoly of legitimate physical force in a territory. His ideal types of authority are traditional, charismatic and legal-rational.
- Descriptive legitimacy is belief that a regime is rightful; normative legitimacy is its actual right to rule. Beetham (1991) criticised Weber for reducing legitimacy to belief, proposing conformity to rules, rules justifiable by shared beliefs, and evidence of consent.
- Simmons (1999): a state may be justified (good to have) without being legitimate over a particular person.

Grounds of obligation
- Consent: Locke's Second Treatise (1689) says enjoying property, or even travelling on the highway, gives tacit consent. Hume ('Of the Original Contract', 1748) replied that a poor peasant's freedom to leave is like that of a man carried aboard ship asleep, who must obey or leap into the sea.
- Hypothetical consent: Dworkin objected that a hypothetical agreement is no agreement at all; any force comes from the underlying reasons.
- Fair play (Hart 1955; Rawls): accepting the benefits of a cooperative scheme obliges one to do one's part. Nozick's public address system example denies that benefits pressed on us create obligations.
- Service conception: Raz's normal justification thesis (1986) says authority is legitimate over someone if following it helps them conform better to reasons that already apply to them. It grounds authority without consent, but piecemeal, person by person and domain by domain.
- Philosophical anarchism: Wolff (1970) argued autonomy is incompatible with state authority; Simmons concludes few if any states are legitimate, though they may be justified.

Critiques of contract
Pateman (The Sexual Contract, 1988) argued the social contract presupposed a sexual contract subordinating women; Charles Mills (The Racial Contract, 1997) argued the actual contract was among whites to treat non-whites as lesser.

Applied example
Marta never consented but uses public roads, a subsidised university place and free health care. Fair-play theorists may say she accepted benefits and owes her share; a Razian points to laws that coordinate action better than she could alone; Simmons would say neither creates general legitimacy, though she may have independent moral reasons to obey many laws.

Exam pitfalls
- Running descriptive and normative legitimacy together.
- Assuming that showing a state is beneficial shows it has authority.
- Treating philosophical anarchism as a call to revolution; it usually allows that many laws should be obeyed for independent reasons.
- Forgetting that tacit consent risks becoming impossible to withhold.

This topic asks what democracy is, whether it protects against domination, and how oppression differs from simple disadvantage.

Models and critics of democracy
- Schumpeter (Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy, 1942): democracy is a method in which leaders compete for the people's vote; citizens choose rulers rather than rule.
- Dahl (1971): real regimes are 'polyarchies' combining inclusion and contestation.
- Deliberative democracy (Habermas, Joshua Cohen): legitimacy rests on public reasoning among free and equal citizens. Young warned that norms of 'reasonable' argument can exclude marginalised speakers.
- Sceptics: Plato's ship of state (Republic VI) reserves rule for those with knowledge; Brennan (Against Democracy, 2016) defends epistocracy, criticised for entrenching inequality.
- Social choice: Condorcet's paradox shows majority voting can cycle; Arrow (1951) showed no ranked voting rule meets a small set of reasonable conditions at once, unsettling the idea of a single popular will.

Majority tyranny
Madison (Federalist No. 10, 1787) sought to control faction through a large representative republic. Tocqueville (Democracy in America) warned of a tyranny of the majority working through conformity of opinion as well as law, and of a soft, paternalist despotism.

Oppression and domination
- Young (Justice and the Politics of Difference, 1990): five faces of oppression, namely exploitation, marginalisation, powerlessness, cultural imperialism and violence. Oppression is structural and group-based and need not have an identifiable oppressor.
- Frye ('Oppression', 1983): the birdcage; no single wire explains the bird's captivity, but the network of barriers does.
- Crenshaw (1989): treating race and sex separately leaves Black women unprotected (intersectionality). The Combahee River Collective (1977) described interlocking systems of oppression.
- Anderson (Private Government, 2017): employers can exercise unaccountable authority over workers, so domination is not confined to the state.

Worked example
Voters rank three options: 35% A>B>C, 33% B>C>A, 32% C>A>B. A beats B by 67% to 33%, B beats C by 68% to 32%, but C beats A by 65% to 35%. The majority preference cycles, so the outcome depends on the order of votes.

Exam pitfalls
- Assuming oppressed groups are always numerical minorities; women are not, and oppression concerns structure rather than numbers.
- Treating Arrow's theorem as proving democracy impossible; it shows every aggregation rule involves trade-offs.
- Listing Young's faces without explaining why oppression is structural.
- Collapsing domination into interference; Anderson and republicans stress unaccountable power even when unused.

Theories of distributive justice ask what people are owed, and whether what matters is the pattern of holdings or the history of how they arose.

Rawls
- A Theory of Justice (1971): parties in the original position choose behind a veil of ignorance about their class, talents, sex and conception of the good.
- Two principles: equal basic liberties; inequalities attached to offices open under fair equality of opportunity and to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged (the difference principle). Lexical priority: liberty first, then fair equality of opportunity, then the difference principle.
- Maximin: choose the option whose worst outcome is best. Harsanyi argued rational choosers would maximise expected utility instead.

Nozick and property
- Entitlement theory (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974): holdings are just if they arise from just acquisition, just transfer or rectification. Justice is historical, not patterned.
- Wilt Chamberlain: voluntary payments upset any pattern, so maintaining one needs continual interference. Taxation of earnings is said to be 'on a par with forced labor'.
- Locke: property by mixing labour with unowned things, limited by the 'enough and as good' and spoilage provisos, with money allowing accumulation. Nozick relies on self-ownership; Cohen argued self-ownership does not settle who owns external resources.

Egalitarian alternatives
- Luck egalitarianism: Dworkin compensates brute luck but lets option luck stand, using a hypothetical auction and insurance market.
- Anderson ('What Is the Point of Equality?', 1999): luck egalitarianism is harsh to the imprudent and demeaning to the unlucky; the aim is to relate as equals.
- Parfit's levelling-down objection motivates prioritarianism; Frankfurt (1987) defends sufficiency.
- Cohen's camping trip (Why Not Socialism?, 2009) defends equality and community as ideals.

Poverty
Singer ('Famine, Affluence, and Morality', 1972): if we can prevent something bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to; distance makes no moral difference. Waldron (1991): every action must happen somewhere, so banning sleeping or washing in public leaves homeless people nowhere they are free to do these things.

Worked example
Policy X gives the poorest fifth £12,000 and the richest £60,000; Policy Y gives £13,000 and £110,000. A simple difference-principle reading favours Y because the worst-off gain, despite greater inequality. If Y is funded by cutting state schools, fair equality of opportunity, which has priority, may rule it out.

Exam pitfalls
- Saying the difference principle forbids inequality; it permits inequalities that benefit the worst-off.
- Forgetting lexical priority when applying Rawls.
- Treating Nozick as opposed to all redistribution; rectification may demand large transfers.
- Mixing up brute and option luck in problem questions.

Four thinkers who give sharply different accounts of order, freedom and the limits of collective action.

Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651)
- Without a common power, life is a war of every one against every one: 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' (ch. 13).
- Causes of quarrel are competition, diffidence and glory, made dangerous by rough equality and scarcity.
- 'Covenants, without the sword, are but words': only an absolute sovereign makes agreements bind. The reply to the Foole (ch. 15) holds that breaking covenants is unreasonable once a sovereign exists.
- Subjects keep an inalienable right of self-preservation, and obligation lasts only as long as protection.

Rousseau
- Discourse on Inequality (1755): amour de soi is natural self-love; amour-propre, the need for others' esteem, breeds vanity and inequality.
- The Social Contract (1762) opens with man born free yet everywhere in chains, and asks what could make this legitimate. The general will aims at the common interest; the will of all is merely the sum of private wills. Sovereignty cannot be represented: the English are free only at elections.

Marx
- Historical materialism (1859 Preface): the economic base conditions the legal and political superstructure.
- Alienated labour (1844): from the product, the activity, species-being and other people.
- 'On the Jewish Question' (1843): political emancipation is real progress but incomplete without human emancipation.
- Exploitation (Capital, 1867): surplus value is extracted even under formally free contracts.
- Eleventh thesis on Feuerbach: philosophers have interpreted the world; the point is to change it.

Hayek
- 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945): knowledge is dispersed and often tacit; prices transmit it, so central planning fails.
- Spontaneous order (cosmos) versus deliberate organisation (taxis).
- The Road to Serfdom (1944): planning leads towards totalitarianism, though he accepted a guaranteed minimum.
- 'Social justice' is a mirage: unintended market outcomes cannot be just or unjust.

Applied comparison
Designing a constitution after civil war, a Hobbesian argues for undivided authority to prevent relapse; a Rousseauian for direct citizen assemblies; a Hayekian for general rules that limit legislative discretion; a Marxist asks whose class interests each design serves.

Exam pitfalls
- Reading Hobbes as defending tyranny without noting the self-preservation limit.
- Treating the general will as majority opinion.
- Presenting Marx's exploitation as a moral complaint about greedy individuals; it is structural.
- Missing common ground: Marx and Hayek both see markets as impersonal orders beyond individual control, but draw opposite conclusions.

notes.h: Overlooked voices: Douglass, Cooper, Nkrumah, Davis
notes.body:
These four thinkers theorised freedom, domination and legitimacy from the standpoint of the enslaved, Black women, the colonised and the incarcerated. Including them challenges a canon that treated such groups as objects of theory rather than its authors.

Frederick Douglass
- Narrative of the Life (1845) presents literacy as a pathway to freedom, and his fight with Edward Covey as the turning point at which he reclaimed his manhood.
- 'What to the Slave is the Fourth of July?' (Rochester, 5 July 1852) exposes the gap between America's professed ideals and slavery: to the enslaved, the celebration is a sham.
- He first followed Garrison in reading the Constitution as pro-slavery, but by around 1851 read it as anti-slavery, which justified political action within the system.
- He signed the Seneca Falls Declaration of Sentiments (1848); The North Star's motto held that right is of no sex.

Anna Julia Cooper
- A Voice from the South (1892) argued that Black women's position made them central to racial and national progress, criticising racism in the white women's movement and sexism among Black male leaders.
- Her claim that when and where the Black woman enters, the whole race enters with her makes Black women's advancement the measure of progress.
- She championed classical higher education against confinement to industrial training.

Kwame Nkrumah
- Led Ghana to independence on 6 March 1957; overthrown in a 1966 coup.
- 'Seek ye first the political kingdom' put political independence first.
- Neo-Colonialism: The Last Stage of Imperialism (1965), echoing Lenin, argued that formal sovereignty can coexist with external economic control. Africa Must Unite (1963) called for continental union; he helped found the OAU in 1963.

Angela Davis
- Women, Race and Class (1981) criticised racism and class blindness in the suffrage and women's movements, for example on sterilisation abuse.
- Are Prisons Obsolete? (2003) analyses the 'prison-industrial complex' and continuities between slavery, convict leasing and mass incarceration, arguing for abolition by building alternatives such as education, health care and decriminalisation.

Applied connections
Nkrumah complicates Weberian legitimacy: a state may monopolise force at home while its policy is directed from outside. Davis challenges liberal accounts of legitimate coercion by asking whether punishment reproduces racial domination.

Exam pitfalls
- Treating these figures as activists without arguments; examiners reward reconstructing their theoretical claims.
- Ignoring change over time (Douglass on the Constitution; Nkrumah on political independence).
- Reducing abolition to opening prison doors rather than building alternatives.
- Anachronism: Cooper anticipates intersectionality but did not use the term.

cards.f: Robert Dahl's pluralist definition of power
cards.b: A has power over B to the extent that A can get B to do something B would not otherwise do. Dahl measured it by observing who prevails in concrete, observable decisions where there is open conflict.

A study of decision-making in New Haven which found that different groups won on different issues (party nominations, urban renewal, education). Dahl concluded that power was dispersed among competing elites rather than held by a single ruling class.

cards.f: Bachrach and Baratz, 'Two Faces of Power' (1962)
cards.b: A critique of pluralism arguing that power is also exercised by keeping issues off the agenda ('non-decision-making'). Studying only observable decisions misses the power to set the terms of what gets decided.

E. E. Schattschneider, in The Semisovereign People (1960), argued that all political organisation favours some conflicts and suppresses others. He also observed that the pluralist 'heavenly chorus' sings with a strong upper-class accent, because organised interests are skewed towards the well-off.

cards.f: Steven Lukes's three dimensions of power
cards.b: In Power: A Radical View (1974), Lukes distinguished (1) decision-making power, (2) agenda-setting or non-decision power, and (3) the power to shape people's wants and beliefs so that conflict never arises. The third dimension operates against people's 'real interests' even where they voice no grievance.

cards.f: The main objection to Lukes's 'real interests'
cards.b: Critics ask who decides what someone's real interests are; if the theorist decides, the concept risks paternalism and is hard to verify empirically. Lukes replied that real interests can be identified by what people would choose under conditions of relative autonomy.

The probability that an actor in a social relationship can carry out their own will despite resistance. Weber distinguished this from domination (Herrschaft), the probability that a command will be obeyed by a given group; stable domination usually rests on belief in its legitimacy.

cards.f: C. Wright Mills, The Power Elite (1956)
cards.b: Argued that post-war American power was concentrated in an interlocking elite drawn from the corporate, military and political hierarchies. Members shared social backgrounds and moved between institutions, challenging the pluralist picture.

Antonio Gramsci (Prison Notebooks, written 1929–35) argued that ruling classes maintain dominance less through force than through consent, by making their worldview appear to be common sense. Civil society institutions such as churches, schools and the press do much of this work.

In Discipline and Punish (1975), Foucault argued that modern power is diffuse and productive: it shapes bodies and selves through surveillance, normalisation and examination rather than simply repressing. Bentham's panopticon models how being visible leads people to discipline themselves.

cards.f: Charles Lindblom on the 'privileged position of business'
cards.b: In Politics and Markets (1977), Lindblom argued that because governments depend on business investment for growth and jobs, business enjoys structural influence over policy without needing to lobby. This is a key version of the 'structural power of capital' thesis.

cards.f: Gilens and Page (2014) on US policy influence
cards.b: Their study of nearly 1,800 policy issues found that economic elites and organised business groups had substantial independent influence on US policy outcomes, while average citizens had little or none. It is widely cited as evidence against majoritarian and pluralist accounts.

Power-over is the capacity to affect or control others; power-to is a capacity to act or achieve outcomes, possibly collectively. Feminist theorists and Hannah Arendt stressed power as collective capacity rather than domination.

cards.f: Hannah Arendt on power and violence
cards.b: In On Violence (1970), Arendt argued that power arises when people act in concert and depends on numbers and support, while violence is instrumental and can destroy power but never create it. Rule by violence alone signals a loss of power.

Berlin's Oxford inaugural lecture distinguished negative liberty (the area within which one is not interfered with by others) from positive liberty (being one's own master, self-government). He warned that positive liberty had historically been used to justify coercion in the name of people's 'true' selves.

Freedom as the absence of interference by other people. On this view, the more an area of action is free from deliberate human obstruction, the freer the agent; inability caused by lack of talent or natural obstacles is not unfreedom.

Freedom as self-mastery or self-realisation: acting on one's rational or authentic will, or participating in collective self-government. It asks 'by whom am I governed?' rather than 'how far am I interfered with?'

Every freedom claim has the form 'x is free from y to do or become z'. MacCallum argued that Berlin's two concepts are really disagreements about how to fill in the three variables, not two distinct concepts.

Philip Pettit (Republicanism, 1997) defines freedom as not being subject to another's capacity to interfere on an arbitrary basis. A slave with a kind master is unfree even if never interfered with, while non-arbitrary law need not reduce freedom.

Recovered a 'neo-Roman' theory of liberty from seventeenth-century English writers: to be free is not to depend on the will of another. Dependence itself, not just actual interference, makes one unfree.

In On Liberty (1859), Mill argued that the only legitimate reason for exercising power over a member of a civilised community against their will is to prevent harm to others. A person's own good is not sufficient warrant.

cards.f: Mill: 'Over himself, over his own body and mind...'
cards.b: '...the individual is sovereign.' The line expresses Mill's defence of self-regarding liberty, though he excluded children and, controversially, 'barbarians' from its scope.

cards.f: Charles Taylor, 'What's Wrong with Negative Liberty' (1979)
cards.b: Distinguished opportunity concepts of freedom (having options open) from exercise concepts (actually exercising control over one's life). Taylor argued negative liberty cannot be held in its crudest form, since we must discriminate between more and less significant freedoms.

If freedom means getting what one wants, a person could become freer by eliminating desires they cannot satisfy. Berlin called this the 'retreat to the inner citadel' and rejected it: a slave who stops wanting freedom does not thereby become free.
In Leviathan (1651, ch. 21), liberty is the absence of external impediments to motion. Hobbes held that acting from fear is still free, so covenants made under threat are valid.

cards.f: Benjamin Constant (1819): liberty of the ancients vs the moderns
cards.b: Ancient liberty was active participation in collective sovereignty; modern liberty is the peaceful enjoyment of private independence. Constant warned against reviving ancient liberty in commercial societies, while still urging citizens not to give up political participation.

cards.f: G. A. Cohen on poverty and freedom
cards.b: Cohen argued that money works like a ticket: lacking it means that if you try to do certain things (board a train, enter a theatre) you will be physically prevented. Poverty therefore restricts negative liberty itself, not just ability.

In The Social Contract (1762, Book I, ch. 7), whoever refuses to obey the general will is to be compelled by the whole body, which means they will be forced to be free. Berlin treated this as a paradigm of the dangers of positive liberty.
In 'Politics as a Vocation' (1919), Weber defined the state as a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory.

cards.f: Weber's three types of legitimate authority
cards.b: Traditional (resting on established custom), charismatic (resting on devotion to an exceptional leader), and legal-rational (resting on belief in the legality of impersonal rules and offices). These are ideal types and are usually mixed in practice.

Descriptive (Weberian) legitimacy concerns whether people believe a regime is rightful; normative legitimacy concerns whether it actually has the right to rule. A regime can be widely believed legitimate without being so.

cards.f: David Beetham, The Legitimation of Power (1991)
cards.b: Criticised Weber for reducing legitimacy to belief. Beetham argued power is legitimate when it conforms to established rules, the rules are justifiable by beliefs shared by rulers and ruled, and there is evidence of consent by the subordinate.

cards.f: Locke on express and tacit consent
cards.b: In the Second Treatise (1689), Locke held that anyone who enjoys property or the benefits of a government's territory, even by lodging or travelling on the highway, gives tacit consent to its laws. Critics argue this makes consent almost impossible to withhold.

Hume denied that most governments rest on consent. He compared the poor peasant's supposed choice to leave his country to that of a man carried on board a ship while asleep who must leap into the sea or obey the master.

Hypothetical consent theories ask what rational people would agree to. Ronald Dworkin objected that a hypothetical agreement is not a weaker kind of real agreement but no agreement at all, so any binding force must come from the reasons behind it.
Those who accept the benefits of a cooperative scheme have an obligation to do their part. It grounds political obligation in reciprocity rather than consent.

In Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), Nozick imagined neighbours setting up a PA system with a duty roster; someone who enjoys the broadcasts without having agreed is not obliged to take a turn. It challenges fair-play obligations imposed by benefits one did not seek.

cards.f: Robert Paul Wolff, In Defense of Anarchism (1970)
cards.b: Argued that the autonomy of the individual, the duty to decide for oneself what to do, is incompatible with the authority of the state. No state can therefore have legitimate authority, a position called philosophical anarchism.

In The Morality of Freedom (1986), an authority is legitimate over someone if that person would better conform to reasons that already apply to them by following its directives than by acting on their own judgement.

Argued that the classical social contract was also a sexual contract establishing men's right of access to women's bodies and labour. Contract theory hides a prior subordination in the language of free agreement.

Argued that the actual social contract of the modern West was a racial one, in which white people agreed among themselves to treat non-whites as lesser and to exploit them. Contractarian ideals presented as universal were in practice racially restricted.

A. John Simmons (1999) argued that a state may be justified (good to have, better than the alternatives) without being legitimate over a particular person, since legitimacy requires a specific transaction such as consent. This supports philosophical anarchism.

In Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942), Schumpeter defined democracy as a method in which leaders acquire the power to decide through a competitive struggle for the people's vote. Citizens choose rulers; they do not rule.

Dahl used 'polyarchy' for real-world regimes that combine wide inclusion (the right to participate) with public contestation (free competition), reserving 'democracy' for an ideal never fully achieved.

In Democracy in America (1835/1840), Tocqueville warned that democratic majorities could oppress minorities, not only through law but by imposing conformity of opinion. He also feared a 'soft' despotism of a paternalistic state over isolated individuals.

Madison argued that the causes of faction cannot be removed without destroying liberty, so their effects must be controlled. A large republic with representation makes it harder for any single majority faction to form and oppress others.

cards.f: Iris Marion Young's five faces of oppression
cards.b: In Justice and the Politics of Difference (1990): exploitation, marginalisation, powerlessness, cultural imperialism and violence. Oppression is structural and group-based, and need not have an identifiable oppressor.
The universalisation of a dominant group's experience and culture as the norm, so that the oppressed group is both stereotyped and rendered invisible. It is one of Young's five faces of oppression.

In 'Oppression' (1983), Frye argued that examining a single wire of a cage cannot explain why the bird cannot escape. Oppression is a network of systematically related barriers, each of which may look harmless alone.

Kimberlé Crenshaw used the term to show that Black women's experiences of discrimination are not captured by treating race and sex as separate categories. Anti-discrimination law that does so leaves those at the intersection unprotected.

A Black feminist statement arguing that the major systems of oppression (racial, sexual, heterosexual and class) are interlocking. It is an early source of 'identity politics' in the sense of organising from one's own oppression.

The view that democratic legitimacy rests on public reasoning among free and equal citizens, not just aggregating preferences by voting. Associated with Habermas and Joshua Cohen; critics such as Young argue its norms of 'reasonable' argument can exclude marginalised speakers.

Majority voting over three or more options can produce cyclical preferences (A beats B, B beats C, C beats A). Arrow (1951) proved that no ranked voting rule can satisfy a small set of reasonable conditions at once, unsettling the idea of a single 'will of the people'.

Argued that many employers exercise sweeping, unaccountable authority over workers' lives, a form of 'private government'. Political theory's focus on the state hides this domination in the workplace.

Jason Brennan argued that because many voters are poorly informed, rule weighted towards the more knowledgeable could produce better outcomes. Critics reply that it entrenches existing inequalities and denies equal political status.

In Book VI of the Republic, Plato pictures a ship whose sailors fight over the helm and dismiss the true navigator as a stargazer. It is usually read as an attack on democracy: rule should belong to those with knowledge, not to whoever wins popular favour.

cards.f: Rawls's original position and veil of ignorance
cards.b: In A Theory of Justice (1971), parties choose principles of justice without knowing their class, talents, sex, or conception of the good. The veil models fairness by stopping people tailoring principles to their own advantage.

(1) Each person has an equal right to the most extensive scheme of equal basic liberties compatible with a like scheme for all. (2) Social and economic inequalities must be attached to offices open to all under fair equality of opportunity and be to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged (the difference principle).

The first principle (liberty) takes strict priority over the second, and fair equality of opportunity takes priority over the difference principle. Basic liberties cannot be traded for economic gains.

Choosing the option whose worst outcome is best. Rawls argued parties in the original position would use it given the high stakes and uncertainty; critics such as Harsanyi argued rational choosers would instead maximise expected utility.
A distribution is just if it arises from just acquisition, just transfer, or rectification of past injustice. Justice is historical, not about matching a pattern or end-state.

Nozick imagines a just starting distribution; a million people freely pay 25 cents each to watch Chamberlain play, making him rich. If each transfer was voluntary, the result is just, so maintaining any pattern would require continual interference with liberty.
Nozick claimed taxation of earnings from labour is on a par with forced labour, since it takes the proceeds of a number of hours of a person's work.

cards.f: Locke's labour theory of property and its proviso
cards.b: In the Second Treatise, one acquires property by mixing one's labour with unowned things, provided 'enough and as good' is left for others and nothing is left to spoil. Locke argued money allowed accumulation beyond the spoilage limit.

Each person owns their body and powers, with rights like those over property. Nozick used it to resist redistribution; G. A. Cohen argued it is compatible with, but does not settle, the question of how external resources should be distributed.

cards.f: Luck egalitarianism and Dworkin's brute vs option luck
cards.b: Inequalities arising from brute luck (unchosen circumstances) should be neutralised; those from option luck (deliberate gambles) may stand. Dworkin's equality of resources uses a hypothetical auction and insurance market to make distribution ambition-sensitive but endowment-insensitive.

cards.f: Anderson, 'What Is the Point of Equality?' (1999)
cards.b: Criticised luck egalitarianism for being harsh to the imprudent and demeaning to the unlucky. Anderson defended democratic (relational) equality: the aim is to end oppression and create a community of equals, not to compensate for bad luck.

If equality matters intrinsically, then making the better-off worse off without benefiting anyone would be in one respect an improvement. Parfit used this to motivate prioritarianism: giving extra weight to benefits for the worse off.
Harry Frankfurt argued that what matters morally is not that everyone has the same, but that each has enough. Critics ask where the threshold lies and whether inequalities above it are irrelevant.

If it is in our power to prevent something bad from happening without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do it. The drowning child example suggests distance makes no moral difference, so the affluent have strong duties to relieve global poverty.

In Why Not Socialism? (2009), Cohen argued that on a camping trip most people would find market-style claims to own and charge for one's contributions repugnant. He used this to defend socialist equality and community as ideals, while admitting the problem of designing them at scale.

cards.f: Waldron, 'Homelessness and the Issue of Freedom' (1991)
cards.b: Jeremy Waldron argued that because every action must happen somewhere, a homeless person with no private place depends on public space; rules banning sleeping or washing in public leave them nowhere they are free to do these things.
Without a common power to keep all in awe, people are in a condition of war of every one against every one. Life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' (Leviathan, 1651, ch. 13).

cards.f: Hobbes's three principal causes of quarrel
cards.b: Competition (for gain), diffidence (distrust, seeking safety) and glory (for reputation). Rough equality of ability and scarcity make pre-emptive attack rational.
'...are but words.' Without a sovereign able to enforce agreements, no one has reason to perform first, so a common power is needed for contracts to bind.

The Foole says breaking covenants can be rational when it pays. Hobbes replies (ch. 15) that once a sovereign exists, breach is never reasonable because no one can count on escaping detection or being received into society afterwards.

Subjects retain an inalienable right of self-preservation: they may resist being killed or wounded and need not incriminate themselves. Obligation lasts only as long as the sovereign can protect them.
'...and everywhere he is in chains' opens The Social Contract (1762). Rousseau's task is not to explain the change but to show what could make it legitimate.

In the Discourse on Inequality (1755), amour de soi is natural, healthy self-love concerned with self-preservation; amour-propre is a socially generated need for others' esteem that breeds vanity, competition and inequality.

cards.f: General will vs will of all (Rousseau)
cards.b: The general will aims at the common interest of citizens as citizens; the will of all is merely the sum of private wills. Sovereignty, the exercise of the general will, cannot be alienated or represented.

cards.f: Rousseau on the English and representation
cards.b: Rousseau claimed the English thought themselves free but were free only during parliamentary elections; once members are elected, the people are enslaved. Hence his rejection of representative sovereignty.

The economic base (forces and relations of production) conditions the legal and political superstructure and forms of consciousness. Set out most compactly in the 1859 Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy.

cards.f: Marx's four aspects of alienated labour (1844)
cards.b: Workers are alienated from the product of their labour, from the activity of labour, from their species-being (their human capacity for free creative activity), and from other people.

Distinguished political emancipation (equal civil rights within the liberal state) from human emancipation. Liberal rights treat people as isolated egoists separated from the community, so political emancipation is real progress but incomplete.

In Capital (vol. 1, 1867), workers sell their labour power for a wage that is less than the value they produce; the difference is surplus value appropriated by capitalists. Exploitation happens even when the wage contract is formally free and fair.
'The philosophers have only interpreted the world, in various ways; the point is to change it.' It expresses Marx's view that theory should serve practical transformation.

cards.f: Hayek, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945)
cards.b: Economic knowledge is dispersed among millions of individuals and often tacit and local. Prices transmit this information, so no central planner could gather what is needed to plan an economy rationally.

A cosmos is an order that results from human action but not human design, such as markets, language or common law; a taxis is a deliberately made organisation. Hayek warned against treating society as if it were a taxis.

In The Mirage of Social Justice (1976, vol. 2 of Law, Legislation and Liberty), Hayek argued that market outcomes are not intended by anyone, so it is a category mistake to call them just or unjust; pursuing social justice requires coercive central direction.
Argued that central economic planning, however well meant, concentrates power and leads towards totalitarianism. Hayek nonetheless accepted a guaranteed minimum of subsistence outside the market.

cards.f: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life (1845)
cards.b: Douglass's first autobiography, describing his enslavement in Maryland, learning to read, and escape. It presents literacy as a 'pathway from slavery to freedom' and his fight with Edward Covey, the farmer to whom he was hired out to be 'broken', as the turning point: 'You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.'

cards.f: 'What to the Slave is the Fourth of July?' (1852)
cards.b: Speech Douglass gave in Rochester, New York, on 5 July 1852. He argued that America's celebration of liberty was a sham to the enslaved and exposed the gap between national ideals and practice.

cards.f: Douglass's changing view of the US Constitution
cards.b: Initially he followed Garrison in seeing the Constitution as pro-slavery; by around 1851 he read it as an anti-slavery document and called it a 'glorious liberty document'. This justified political action within the constitutional system.
Douglass attended the Seneca Falls Convention (1848) and signed its Declaration of Sentiments, supporting women's suffrage. His newspaper The North Star carried the motto that right is of no sex.

cards.f: Anna Julia Cooper, A Voice from the South (1892)
cards.b: Collected essays arguing that Black women's distinctive position made them essential to the progress of their race and nation. Cooper criticised both racism in the white women's movement and sexism among Black male leaders.

Cooper wrote that only the Black woman can say that when and where she enters with dignity, the whole race enters with her. The point is that Black women's advancement is the measure of racial progress, not an afterthought.

Cooper championed higher, classical education for Black women and men against the view that they should be confined to industrial training. As principal of M Street High School in Washington, D.C., she prepared students for elite colleges.
Led the Gold Coast to independence as Ghana on 6 March 1957, becoming its first Prime Minister and later President. A leading Pan-Africanist, he was overthrown in a 1966 coup.

In Neo-Colonialism: The Last Stage of Imperialism, a state may have formal independence and the trappings of sovereignty while its economy, and therefore its policy, is directed from outside. The title consciously echoes Lenin's Imperialism (1917).

Nkrumah argued in Africa Must Unite (1963) that small, divided African states could not escape neo-colonial dependence; only political and economic union of the continent could secure real independence. He helped found the Organisation of African Unity in 1963.

cards.f: Nkrumah's 'Seek ye first the political kingdom'
cards.b: Nkrumah's slogan that political independence must come first, after which economic and social progress would follow. His later work on neo-colonialism suggests he came to see political independence as insufficient on its own.

cards.f: Angela Davis, Women, Race and Class (1981)
cards.b: Examined how race and class shaped women's oppression, criticising racism in the US suffrage and women's movements and their neglect of Black and working-class women, for example on sterilisation abuse.

Argued for prison abolition, analysing the 'prison-industrial complex' and the continuities between slavery, convict leasing and mass incarceration. Abolition means building alternatives (education, health care, decriminalisation) rather than only reforming prisons.
A student of Herbert Marcuse and a Communist Party member, Davis was dismissed from UCLA in 1969 and later tried on charges linked to a 1970 courtroom attack; she was acquitted in 1972.

They theorised freedom, domination and legitimacy from the standpoint of the enslaved, Black women, the colonised and the incarcerated. Including them challenges a canon that treated those groups as objects of theory rather than authors of it.

questions.q: Which thinker defined power as A getting B to do something that B would not otherwise do?
questions.why: This is Dahl's behavioural, pluralist definition from 'The Concept of Power' (1957). It focuses on observable conflict over particular decisions.

questions.q: A city council never debates rent control because councillors assume landlords would block it, so the proposal never reaches the agenda. Which account of power best captures this?
options: Bachrach and Baratz's second face of power
Arendt's concept of power as acting in concert
questions.why: Keeping an issue off the agenda is 'non-decision-making', the second face of power. Dahl's method would see no conflict and so no exercise of power.

questions.q: Explain what Steven Lukes means by the third dimension of power and give one example.
markScheme: Third dimension: power to shape people's preferences, beliefs or wants so that conflict does not surface
Operates against people's 'real interests', even when they express no grievance
Relevant example, e.g. advertising, ideology or socialisation leading a group to accept its subordination as natural
questions.modelAnswer: Lukes's third dimension is the power to shape what people want and believe, so that no observable conflict or grievance ever arises. Unlike the first dimension (winning decisions) or the second (keeping issues off the agenda), it works by influencing consciousness itself, against people's real interests. For example, if workers in a company town have absorbed the belief that pollution is simply the price of having jobs, they may never campaign against it, even though they would object if they understood their situation and could choose more freely. On Lukes's view, the absence of complaint here is itself an effect of power.

questions.q: Outline Charles Lindblom's argument about the 'privileged position of business' and explain why it challenges pluralism.
markScheme: Governments depend on private investment for growth, jobs and tax revenue
So policymakers anticipate business reactions and avoid policies that would harm business confidence
Business influence is therefore structural: it does not require lobbying or visible conflict
Challenges pluralism, which treats business as one interest group among many competing on roughly equal terms
questions.modelAnswer: Lindblom argued in Politics and Markets (1977) that in market economies key decisions about investment, employment and growth are taken by private firms. Since governments are judged on economic performance and need tax revenue, they must keep business confident and willing to invest. Policymakers therefore anticipate what business wants and avoid measures that might trigger disinvestment, often without any lobbying taking place. This gives business a structural advantage. It undermines pluralism, which pictures business as one interest group among many competing openly, because the advantage operates before and outside the visible contest of groups.

questions.q: Scenario: In the town of Eastbridge, a proposed incinerator is to be built next to Fenwick Estate, a low-income housing estate. A public consultation receives 40 responses: 30 from residents of the wealthy Hillside ward (which had successfully opposed an earlier site there), and 10 from Fenwick. The council approves the Fenwick site with no visible protest. A local survey later finds that 70% of Fenwick residents did not know the consultation was happening, and many say 'there's no point complaining, nobody listens to us'. Using the three dimensions of power, analyse who exercised power in Eastbridge and how. Which dimension best explains the outcome?
markScheme: Explains Dahl's one-dimensional view and what it would observe (no open conflict, decision appears uncontested)
Identifies Hillside's earlier victory as an observable first-dimension exercise of power
Explains the second dimension: agenda-setting and the mobilisation of bias in how the consultation was run and publicised
Uses the data: 30 vs 10 responses, 70% unaware, as evidence of unequal access to the decision process
Explains the third dimension: resignation and fatalism ('no point complaining') as shaped preferences
Discusses the difficulty of proving real interests and the counterfactual (what residents would want if informed)
Considers alternative explanations (e.g. rational apathy, lack of resources) rather than power
Reaches a reasoned judgement about which dimension is most explanatory
Clear structure applying theory to the facts rather than describing theories in the abstract
questions.modelAnswer:
A one-dimensional, Dahlian analysis would find little to explain. The council took a decision, there was no visible protest from Fenwick, and so no one can be said to have prevailed over anyone else in this case. The only clear first-dimension exercise of power is Hillside's earlier success in defeating a site in its own ward, an observable contest it won.

The second dimension reveals more. Bachrach and Baratz argued that power is also exercised by shaping the procedures through which issues are decided. Here the consultation drew three times as many responses from Hillside as from Fenwick, and 70% of Fenwick residents did not know it existed. Whether by design or by default, the process favoured groups with the time, information and networks to take part, an instance of Schattschneider's mobilisation of bias. The Fenwick site was effectively chosen before any contest could happen.

The third dimension explains the residents' silence. Lukes would treat the remark 'there's no point complaining' as evidence that repeated exclusion has shaped residents' expectations so that grievance does not turn into action. Their apparent acceptance cannot be read as consent; it is plausibly against their real interest in clean air, which we can infer from what wealthier residents chose when they had the chance.

There are objections. Survey answers might reflect a rational judgement about the costs of participation rather than distorted preferences, and attributing power to particular actors is hard when no one may have intended the outcome. This is where structural accounts help: inequality can produce outcomes without a single identifiable agent.

On balance the second dimension does most explanatory work, since the data show unequal access to the procedure itself. The third dimension then explains why that inequality persists without challenge. A purely pluralist reading would misdescribe the case as consensus.

questions.q: 'Pluralists were right that power is dispersed in modern democracies; their critics confuse inequality of resources with inequality of power.' Discuss.
markScheme: Sets out the pluralist position (Dahl, Who Governs?) and its method of studying observable decisions
Gives the pluralist's strongest case: different groups win in different issue areas; resources are non-cumulative
Explains the second-face critique (Bachrach and Baratz; Schattschneider) and its implications for method
Explains Lukes's third dimension and the real-interests problem
Considers structural critiques (Lindblom; Mills) and empirical evidence such as Gilens and Page (2014)
Engages directly with the proposition's distinction between resources and power (Dahl himself distinguished potential from actual power)
Evaluates whether unequal resources reliably convert into unequal outcomes
Considers neo-pluralism (later Dahl and Lindblom conceding business privilege)
Reaches a clear, justified conclusion
Well-structured argument rather than a list of theories
questions.modelAnswer:
The proposition defends pluralism by drawing a line that Dahl himself drew: having resources such as money or status is only potential power, and power is shown only when someone prevails in a contested decision. Who Governs? (1961) found that in New Haven different actors won in different issue areas, and that advantages in one resource did not translate automatically into dominance overall. On this view critics who point to inequality of wealth are pointing to the wrong thing.

The distinction is real but does less work than the proposition claims. First, Bachrach and Baratz showed that power is also exercised in deciding which issues are contested at all. If the only issues studied are those that reach the agenda, a method based on observable decisions will see dispersal precisely where agenda control is concentrated. Resources matter here not because they automatically win votes but because they shape what is discussable. Schattschneider's point that the 'heavenly chorus' of interest groups has an upper-class accent makes the same claim about who gets organised.

Second, structural critics argue that resources convert into power without any contest. Lindblom's privileged position of business means governments pre-emptively serve investors. Notably, Dahl and Lindblom later moved towards this 'neo-pluralist' view, which is a significant concession from inside the tradition.

Third, the empirical record has moved against pluralism. Gilens and Page's (2014) analysis of nearly 1,800 US policy issues found that economic elites and business groups had substantial independent influence on outcomes while average citizens had little. That is evidence about outcomes, not just resources, so it meets the pluralist on their own terms.

Lukes's third dimension is the weakest stick with which to beat pluralism, because claims about 'real interests' are hard to test. But the critique does not depend on it.

The proposition is therefore right that resources and power should not be conflated, but wrong to conclude that power is dispersed. The best evidence, from agenda-setting, structural dependence and policy outcomes, suggests that unequal resources do translate into unequal power, though less mechanically than crude elite theory assumes.

questions.q: 'If power is everywhere, as Foucault suggests, then the concept loses its critical edge: we can no longer distinguish domination from ordinary social life.' Assess this objection with reference to at least two other theories of power.
markScheme: Accurate account of Foucault's view of power as diffuse, productive and capillary (Discipline and Punish; disciplinary power, panopticon)
States the objection precisely: a concept that applies everywhere cannot discriminate between cases or ground critique
Considers the normative critique (e.g. Habermas, Fraser) that Foucault lacks a standard to say why domination is bad
Compares with Lukes: the third dimension keeps a critical standard via real interests, at the cost of verification problems
Compares with Weber, Arendt or Pettit to show how other accounts draw lines (legitimacy, power vs violence, arbitrariness)
Considers Foucault's own responses: distinction between power relations and states of domination in later work; resistance is internal to power
Evaluates whether description of power can be separated from normative evaluation
Considers whether the ubiquity of power is a strength for analysing modern institutions (prisons, schools, medicine)
Reaches a nuanced, justified conclusion
Sophisticated structure and precise use of concepts
questions.modelAnswer:
Foucault's Discipline and Punish (1975) argued that modern power works less through sovereign commands than through surveillance, normalisation and examination spread across prisons, schools, hospitals and workplaces. Power is not only repressive but productive: it makes certain kinds of selves. The objection is that if every social relation is a relation of power, the concept no longer picks anything out, and we cannot say why some arrangements are oppressive and others benign.

The objection has force. Critics such as Nancy Fraser argued that Foucault's descriptions are full of critical energy but lack an explicit standard explaining what is wrong with discipline. Without some idea of autonomy, consent or justice, the analysis seems to say only that things are arranged one way rather than another.

Other theories keep the critical edge by building in such a standard. Lukes defines power as affecting someone contrary to their interests, so power is by definition something that needs justification; the cost is that he must identify real interests, which invites charges of paternalism. Pettit's republicanism distinguishes arbitrary from non-arbitrary interference: a teacher or a law may affect us without dominating us if it is controlled by our interests. Arendt goes further by separating power, as people acting together, from violence, which shows that a concept of power need not be negative at all.

Foucault has resources of his own. In later interviews he distinguished fluid power relations, which are an unavoidable feature of social life and contain possibilities of resistance, from 'states of domination' in which relations are frozen and resistance is blocked. This restores a distinction close to the one the objection says is lost. His genealogies also have critical force of a different kind: by showing that practices we treat as natural have contingent histories, they open them to challenge.

The best conclusion is that the objection succeeds against Foucault's early, unqualified formulations but not against a careful reading. Ubiquity is useful for analysis, since it directs attention to institutions that state-centred theories ignore. But critique needs an evaluative standard, and the most persuasive position combines Foucault's descriptive breadth with an explicit norm such as non-domination.

questions.q: In 'Two Concepts of Liberty' (1958), negative liberty is best described as:
options: Freedom to participate in collective self-government
The absence of interference by other people
Acting in accordance with one's rational true self
Having the resources to achieve one's goals
questions.why: Berlin defines negative liberty as the area within which a person can act unobstructed by others. Self-government and the 'true self' belong to positive liberty.

questions.q: A worker on a zero-hours contract is never actually disciplined, but her manager can cancel her shifts at will for any reason. On which account is she clearly unfree?
options: Hobbesian liberty as absence of external impediments
Berlin's negative liberty as actual non-interference
questions.why: For Pettit and Skinner, being subject to another's arbitrary power to interfere makes one unfree even if they never use it. Pure non-interference accounts would say she is not currently interfered with.

questions.q: State Mill's harm principle and identify one difficulty in applying it.
markScheme: Power may be exercised over an individual against their will only to prevent harm to others
A person's own good, physical or moral, is not a sufficient reason
Difficulty identified, e.g. defining harm (offence? indirect or cumulative harms?) or the self-regarding/other-regarding distinction
questions.modelAnswer: Mill's harm principle, from On Liberty (1859), holds that the only legitimate reason for exercising power over any member of a civilised community against their will is to prevent harm to others. Protecting a person from themselves is not sufficient warrant, though we may argue with or persuade them. A central difficulty is defining harm. Almost any action affects others in some way, so the line between self-regarding and other-regarding conduct is unstable; heavy drinking, for example, may affect family members and public services. If offence counts as harm, the principle loses its liberal force; if it does not, it may be too permissive.

questions.q: Explain MacCallum's triadic analysis of freedom and how it is meant to dissolve Berlin's distinction.
markScheme: Every freedom claim has the form: agent x is free from constraint y to do or become z
Freedom is therefore always both 'from' and 'to'; there is one concept, not two
Apparent negative/positive disputes are disagreements about the range of the variables: who counts as the agent, what counts as a constraint, what counts as an action
Example, e.g. whether poverty or internal compulsion counts as a constraint
questions.modelAnswer: Gerald MacCallum (1967) argued that every intelligible claim about freedom has three parts: an agent x is free from some constraint y to do or become z. Freedom is thus always both freedom from something and freedom to do something, so Berlin's split into negative and positive concepts is misleading. What really separates theorists is how they fill in the variables. They disagree about what the agent is (an empirical self or a 'true' rational self), what counts as a constraint (only deliberate human interference, or also poverty, ignorance or addiction), and which actions matter. For example, whether a poor person is unfree to buy medicine depends on whether lack of money counts as a constraint.

questions.q: Scenario: The government of Veridia proposes three policies. (A) A 20% tax on sugary drinks to reduce obesity among adults. (B) Compulsory voting, with a £50 fine for not voting. (C) A law guaranteeing all workers a right to challenge dismissal before an independent tribunal, which employers say limits their freedom to hire and fire. For each policy, assess whether it increases or reduces freedom according to (i) negative liberty, (ii) positive liberty and (iii) republican non-domination. Which conception gives the most convincing overall verdict?
markScheme: Accurate definitions of negative, positive and republican freedom
Policy A: reduces negative liberty for consumers in a small way; Mill-style anti-paternalism; positive liberty could support it as helping people act on considered rather than impulsive preferences

Policy B: interference reduces negative liberty; positive liberty as civic participation (Rousseau/Constant) could see it as freedom-enhancing; danger Berlin identifies of 'forcing' people towards their true selves
Policy C: employers lose some negative liberty; workers gain protection from arbitrary power, so it increases freedom on the republican view even though it adds interference
Notes that republicans accept non-arbitrary law as non-freedom-reducing
Recognises that conceptions give different verdicts and explains why
Evaluative conclusion about which conception best tracks our considered judgements
Clear structure, policy by policy or conception by conception
questions.modelAnswer:
Negative liberty, in Berlin's sense, is the absence of interference by others. Positive liberty is self-mastery or self-government. Republican freedom, for Pettit, is the absence of domination, meaning subjection to another's capacity to interfere arbitrarily.

Policy A, the sugar tax, slightly reduces negative liberty by making one option costlier, and a Millian would object that adults' self-regarding choices are their own business. A positive-liberty theorist might argue the tax helps people act on their considered wish to be healthy rather than on impulse. Republicans would ask whether the tax is non-arbitrary: if it is passed by a democratic process that tracks citizens' interests, it is not domination and so does not reduce freedom.

Policy B, compulsory voting, clearly reduces negative liberty, since abstention is penalised. A participatory conception of positive liberty, drawing on Rousseau or Constant's 'liberty of the ancients', might treat voting as an exercise of collective self-rule. This is exactly the move Berlin feared: coercing people in the name of a freedom they have not chosen. Republicans are mixed; civic participation helps keep government under popular control, but a fine is a modest interference whose justification depends on whether it really guards against domination.

Policy C shows the conceptions diverging most sharply. Employers lose negative liberty to dismiss at will. But workers who can be dismissed for any reason live at the mercy of their employer's will, which republicans count as domination even if the power is rarely used. A tribunal right makes that power non-arbitrary, so it increases freedom overall on the republican view.

Negative liberty is the clearest measure but gives counter-intuitive verdicts in C, treating the employer's loss as a loss of freedom and missing the worker's vulnerability. Positive liberty risks justifying paternalism, as in B. The republican conception gives the most convincing overall verdict, since it explains why some laws restrict freedom and others protect it, though its reliance on 'arbitrariness' needs careful specification.

questions.q: 'Berlin was right: the history of positive liberty is a history of tyranny wearing the mask of emancipation.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explains Berlin's argument: the divided self, the 'true' or rational self, and the slide to coercion in its name
Uses Rousseau's 'forced to be free' and/or other historical examples Berlin invokes
Acknowledges Berlin's concession that negative liberty can also be abused (laissez-faire) and that both are genuine values
Counter-argument: the slide is not logically necessary; positive liberty need not posit a true self known by others
Uses Taylor's exercise-concept or MacCallum's critique
Considers republican freedom as a third option that avoids both problems
Considers the costs of rejecting positive liberty, e.g. ignoring internal obstacles, ideology or lack of resources (link to Lukes or Cohen)
Evaluates whether the problem lies in the concept or in its political use
Justified conclusion
Coherent structure and accurate use of texts
questions.modelAnswer:
Berlin's warning was that positive liberty splits the self into a higher, rational self and a lower, empirical one driven by passion. Once this is accepted, others who claim to know what my rational self wants can coerce me and call it liberation. Rousseau's remark that a citizen who refuses the general will may be 'forced to be free' is Berlin's paradigm, and he linked this logic to twentieth-century authoritarian movements that claimed to realise the people's true will.

The proposition overstates Berlin. He did not claim that positive liberty is a mask; he said it is a genuine human value whose distortion has historically been more dangerous. He also acknowledged that negative liberty had been used to defend exploitation, since freedom to do as one likes means little to people without the means to act.

The deeper objection is that the slide to tyranny is not logically required. Charles Taylor argued that freedom as the exercise of control over one's life is coherent and indispensable, because we naturally judge that someone ruled by a compulsion they repudiate is less free. Recognising internal obstacles does not entail that the state knows my true will better than I do. MacCallum likewise showed that the dispute concerns how to specify agents and constraints, not two rival ideas.

Republicans offer a third route. Pettit and Skinner locate unfreedom in domination, which avoids appeal to a true self while still explaining why dependence on another's will is a loss of freedom. And rejecting positive liberty wholesale has costs: it makes it hard to explain how ideology or poverty constrain people, points pressed by Lukes and G. A. Cohen.

The proposition is thus half true. History does show positive liberty being abused, and Berlin's warning about claims to know others' real wills remains valuable. But the danger lies in a particular political use, the paternalist claim to speak for the true self, not in the ideal of self-government as such. A defensible conception of freedom needs to include it, suitably limited by pluralism.

questions.q: 'Poverty is not a lack of freedom; it is a lack of the ability to use freedom.' Critically assess this claim, drawing on liberal, republican and Marxist arguments.
markScheme: Identifies the claim as the standard liberal/libertarian view (e.g. Berlin's distinction between liberty and the conditions of liberty; Hayek)
Explains the reasoning: only deliberate human interference counts as unfreedom; inability is a separate matter
Explains G. A. Cohen's argument that money functions like a ticket and lack of it exposes people to interference
Uses Waldron on homelessness or similar as an applied illustration
Republican argument: poverty creates dependence and so domination (e.g. on employers, landlords, benefit officials)
Marxist argument: formal freedom of the wage contract conceals structural compulsion to sell labour power; exploitation
Considers replies: e.g. if everything that limits options is unfreedom, the concept becomes indistinct; whether markets are human arrangements
Rawls's distinction between liberty and its 'worth' as a middle position
Reaches a precise, defended conclusion
Sophisticated, well-organised argument with accurate references
questions.modelAnswer:
The claim expresses a familiar liberal position. Berlin argued that being unable to do something because of poverty is not, strictly, unfreedom, unless the poverty results from others' deliberate arrangements; Rawls similarly distinguished liberty from its 'worth'. Hayek insisted that freedom means absence of coercion and that confusing it with power or wealth invites endless state intervention. The motivation is clarity: if every limitation is unfreedom, the concept stops meaning anything.

G. A. Cohen gives the most powerful internal critique. Money, he argued, works like a ticket. If a person without money tries to board a train or take food from a shop, they will be physically stopped by other people. So lack of money does not merely leave someone unable to act; it exposes them to interference, which is unfreedom on the negative conception itself. Waldron's analysis of homelessness illustrates the point. Every act must be done somewhere, and someone with no private place is free to sleep or wash only where public rules allow, so a ban on these acts in public leaves them nowhere free to perform basic functions.

Republicans reach a similar conclusion by another route. Poverty creates dependence on employers, landlords or officials who can make one's life worse at will. On Pettit's account, living at the mercy of such discretion is domination, even if it is rarely exercised.

Marxists go further. Marx argued that the wage relation is formally free, as workers can refuse any particular job, yet they are structurally compelled to sell their labour power because they lack means of production. The language of freedom in the market thus hides a form of compulsion and the extraction of surplus value.

The liberal can reply that these arguments stretch freedom to cover any disadvantage. But Cohen's argument does not: it relies only on interference, the liberal's own criterion, and on the fact that property rules are enforced by people. Rawls's 'worth of liberty' concedes much of the substance while keeping the vocabulary.

The claim should therefore be rejected in its strong form. Poverty is partly a lack of freedom, because it is constituted by enforceable rules that exclude people, and it typically produces domination. The ability/freedom distinction is useful at the margins but cannot carry the political conclusion it is usually meant to support.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of Weber's three ideal types of legitimate authority?
questions.why: Weber's types are traditional, charismatic and legal-rational. Contract-based legitimacy belongs to social contract theory, not Weber's typology.

questions.q: Hume compared a poor peasant's supposed freedom to leave his country to a man carried aboard a ship while asleep. What was Hume's point?
options: Emigration should be a protected right
Tacit consent through residence is not genuine consent when exit is practically impossible
Governments are legitimate only if founded on an original contract
Political obligation arises from the benefits of protection
questions.why: Hume's target is Locke-style tacit consent: staying is not a free choice if leaving is unrealistic. He grounded allegiance instead in custom and utility, not in benefits as a form of consent.

questions.q: Distinguish descriptive from normative legitimacy and explain why the distinction matters.
markScheme: Descriptive legitimacy: whether people believe a regime or authority is rightful (Weber)
Normative legitimacy: whether the authority actually has a right to rule or to be obeyed
The two can come apart: a regime may be believed legitimate through propaganda or ideology without being so, or be rightful but unpopular
Matters because empirical stability does not settle moral questions about obligation; also Beetham's critique that belief alone is insufficient
questions.modelAnswer: Descriptive legitimacy, associated with Weber, is a social fact: an authority is legitimate if those subject to it believe it has the right to rule. Normative legitimacy is a moral question: whether the authority really does have that right, so that its commands create reasons or duties to obey. The two can diverge. A regime might secure belief in its legitimacy through propaganda, as Gramsci's analysis of hegemony suggests, without deserving it; another might be just but distrusted. The distinction matters because a political scientist explaining stability needs the first, while a citizen deciding whether to obey needs the second. Beetham argued that Weber's purely belief-based account blurs this.

questions.q: Explain Raz's normal justification thesis and assess whether it shows how a state can have legitimate authority without consent.
markScheme: States the thesis: authority is legitimate if the subject better conforms to reasons that already apply by following its directives than by acting on their own judgement
Explains pre-emption: authoritative directives replace rather than add to the subject's own reasons
Explains how this answers Wolff's autonomy objection: deferring can itself be what reason requires
Notes the thesis is piecemeal: authority may be legitimate over some people in some domains, not over everyone in all matters
Evaluative point, e.g. it cannot justify the general, comprehensive authority states claim, or it neglects the democratic/procedural value of consent
questions.modelAnswer: Raz's normal justification thesis holds that A has legitimate authority over B if B would better conform to reasons that already apply to B by following A's directives than by trying to act on those reasons directly. Directives then pre-empt B's own balancing of reasons. This answers Wolff's anarchism, since deferring to an expert or coordinator, as with traffic rules, can be what reason recommends. But the thesis is piecemeal: a pharmacologist may do better following her own judgement than the drug regulator's, so authority varies by person and domain. Raz thus justifies less than the general authority states claim, and critics add that he neglects the value of having a say in the rules.

questions.q: Scenario: Marta, aged 24, was born in the country of Corvia and has never voted, signed an oath, or been asked to agree to its constitution. She uses public roads, attends a state university on a subsidised place and receives free health care. She argues that, since she never consented, she has no obligation to obey Corvia's laws, including a new tax she regards as unfair. Assess Marta's argument using consent theory (express, tacit and hypothetical) and the principle of fair play. Does she have a political obligation to pay the tax?
markScheme: Explains express consent and notes Marta has given none
Explains Locke's tacit consent via residence and use of property/highways and applies it to Marta's use of roads etc.
Uses Hume's ship objection to show that residence is not free consent when exit is costly
Explains hypothetical consent and Dworkin's objection that hypothetical agreement does not bind
Explains fair play (Hart/Rawls) and applies to Marta's acceptance of university and health benefits
Uses Nozick's PA system objection and the distinction between accepting and merely receiving benefits (Simmons)
Distinguishes whether the tax is unfair from whether Marta has a general obligation to obey
Reaches a reasoned conclusion on whether some obligation exists
Clear application of each theory to the facts
questions.modelAnswer:
Marta is right that she has given no express consent: she has never promised, sworn or voted. The question is whether other forms of consent, or a non-consensual principle, bind her.

Locke argued that anyone who enjoys a government's territory, even by travelling on the highway, gives tacit consent to its laws. Marta uses roads and public services, so on Locke's account she is bound. But Hume's reply is powerful. Consent requires a real option to refuse, and for most people leaving their country is like a sleeper carried aboard a ship being told he may leap into the sea. Marta has nowhere obvious to go and did not choose to be born in Corvia, so treating residence as consent stretches the concept until it is empty.

Hypothetical consent fares little better. Even if a rational person would agree to Corvia's laws, Dworkin observes that a hypothetical agreement is not an agreement. Its force would come from the reasons the laws are good, not from any consent.

Fair play is more promising. Hart and Rawls argued that those who accept the benefits of a fair cooperative scheme must share its burdens. Marta has not merely received benefits like clean air but actively taken up a subsidised university place and health care. Nozick's public address example shows that one cannot be bound simply by having benefits thrust upon one, and Simmons stresses that only accepted benefits count.
