Marta's case falls on the stronger side of that line because she sought these goods.

Two caveats follow. Fair play applies only if the scheme is reasonably fair, and the obligation is to do one's share in general, not to accept every particular law. Marta may have grounds to campaign against or challenge the new tax.

Overall, consent theories fail to bind her, but fair play gives her a defeasible obligation to contribute, which probably includes paying the tax, while leaving room for protest.

questions.q: 'The social contract tradition does not explain political legitimacy; it disguises domination as agreement.' Discuss with reference to Pateman and Charles Mills.
markScheme: Outlines the social contract tradition's aim (Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau): legitimacy from the agreement of free and equal individuals
Explains Pateman's sexual contract: the original contract presupposed men's patriarchal right over women; marriage and employment contracts as subordination
Explains Mills's racial contract: actual contract among whites; personhood racially restricted; ties to colonialism and slavery
Distinguishes the descriptive/historical charge from the normative charge against the ideal itself
Considers the reply that ideals can be extended (Mills himself later argued for using contract theory correctively, e.g. 'Black radical liberalism')
Considers Hume's point that historical contracts never happened, so the theory was always normative
Evaluates whether the idea of consent can be rescued or whether it is intrinsically flawed
Reaches a clear conclusion
Structured, accurate engagement with texts
questions.modelAnswer:
Classical contract theory explains legitimacy by imagining free and equal individuals agreeing to form a political order. Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau differed on the terms, but all used agreement to explain why political power can be rightful.

Carole Pateman argued in The Sexual Contract (1988) that the story is incomplete. The contract among men to establish civil society presupposed a prior sexual contract securing men's access to women. Marriage, in which wives historically lost legal personality, and employment, in which workers submit to command, show that contract can be a mechanism for creating subordination, not ending it. The language of free agreement disguises this.

Charles Mills's The Racial Contract (1997) extended the argument. The real contract of modern Western politics, he claimed, was among white people, who agreed to treat non-white people as less than full persons and to justify colonial expropriation and slavery. Locke, who defended free consent while being involved in colonial enterprises, illustrates the gap between ideal and practice.

These critiques are strongest as historical and ideological claims. They show that 'everyone' in contract theory meant some people, and that agreement language legitimised real domination. It is harder to see that they refute the normative ideal. Hume had already pointed out that actual contracts rarely founded states, so the tradition was largely a test of justification rather than history. Rawls's hypothetical contract explicitly removes knowledge of race and sex.

Pateman's answer is that contract itself, as exchange of obedience for protection, is structurally prone to subordination, so extending it is not enough. Mills took a different line: he later argued that contract theory could be used correctively, to model what justice requires given a history of racial domination.

The proposition is persuasive about how the tradition functioned, but too strong as a claim about the idea of consent. The critiques show that legitimacy cannot be read off formal agreement alone; it requires attention to the background power relations in which agreement takes place. Mills's corrective use seems more defensible than wholesale rejection.

questions.q: 'Since no actual state meets the conditions for legitimate authority, we should all be philosophical anarchists.' Critically evaluate this claim.
markScheme: Defines philosophical anarchism (Wolff; Simmons) and distinguishes it from political anarchism: no general duty to obey, but no duty to overthrow either
Sets out Wolff's autonomy argument
Sets out Simmons's argument that consent, tacit consent, fair play and gratitude all fail to ground general obligation; justification vs legitimacy
Considers Raz's normal justification thesis as a partial reply
Considers natural duty views (Rawls's natural duty of justice; Waldron's particularity problem)
Considers democratic or associative responses (e.g. Dworkin's associative obligations)
Evaluates the practical difference philosophical anarchism makes: people may still have moral reasons to obey most laws
Addresses the 'particularity' problem: why this state rather than any just state
Reaches a defensible conclusion
Sophisticated argument structure
questions.modelAnswer:
Philosophical anarchism holds that no existing state has legitimate authority, meaning a general right to be obeyed that correlates with citizens' duty to obey. Unlike political anarchists, philosophical anarchists need not call for the state's abolition. Wolff argued that autonomy requires each person to decide for themselves what to do, so submitting to authority as such is incompatible with moral agency. Simmons argued more cautiously that each candidate ground of obligation fails for most people: express consent is rare, tacit consent through residence is not voluntary, fair play applies only to accepted benefits, and gratitude does not generate duties of obedience. A state can be justified, good to have, without being legitimate over any particular person.

Several replies are available. Raz shows that deferring to authority can be what reason requires, which answers Wolff. But Raz's account is piecemeal and arguably concedes the anarchist's point that no state has the comprehensive authority it claims.

Natural duty views hold that we have a duty to support just institutions that apply to us, whether or not we consent. Rawls's natural duty of justice is the classic example. The challenge, which Simmons calls the particularity problem, is to explain why this duty binds me to my own state rather than to any just institution. Waldron responded that institutions that apply to us, by claiming jurisdiction over us, create special demands.

Associative theories, such as Dworkin's, argue that political obligations, like family obligations, arise from membership in a community of equal concern rather than from choice. Critics find this too accommodating of unchosen and possibly oppressive memberships.

The practical stakes are smaller than they appear. A philosophical anarchist still has strong moral reasons to obey laws against violence or fraud, because those acts are wrong anyway, and reasons to support justified institutions. What they deny is that the law's say-so adds a further reason.

I conclude that the anarchist case is stronger than often thought, especially against consent theory, but the conclusion should be qualified. Natural duty accounts, supplemented by a response to particularity, show that we can have duties to support just states that claim us, even if not a general duty to obey every law. A moderate position, legitimate authority in some domains but not a comprehensive duty to obey, is more defensible than either full anarchism or traditional statism.

questions.q: Who defined democracy as an institutional arrangement in which leaders acquire power through a competitive struggle for the people's vote?
questions.why: This is Schumpeter's minimalist or 'competitive elitist' definition from Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942).

questions.q: Which of the following is one of Iris Marion Young's 'five faces of oppression'?
questions.why: Young's five faces are exploitation, marginalisation, powerlessness, cultural imperialism and violence. The other options come from Marx, Engels or Durkheim.

questions.q: Voters rank three options: 35% prefer A>B>C, 33% prefer B>C>A and 32% prefer C>A>B. Under pairwise majority voting, what happens?
options: A wins, since it has the most first preferences
B wins, since it beats both others head-to-head
There is a cycle: A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A
C wins, since it is never ranked last by a majority
questions.why: A beats B 67–33, B beats C 68–32, and C beats A 65–35, so there is no Condorcet winner. This is Condorcet's paradox.

questions.q: What did Tocqueville mean by the 'tyranny of the majority'?
markScheme: The danger that a democratic majority oppresses minorities
Not only through law and political institutions but through social pressure and conformity of opinion
He thought this pressure on thought could be stronger in democratic America than under European monarchies, and argued for safeguards such as associations, local government and the judiciary
questions.modelAnswer: In Democracy in America, Tocqueville warned that where the majority is sovereign it may oppress minorities, since there is no higher power to appeal to. He emphasised not only legal oppression but the pressure of public opinion: the majority sets the boundaries of acceptable thought, so dissenters face social exclusion rather than prison. He claimed that he knew of no country with less independence of mind than America. As counterweights he valued civil associations, local self-government, the legal profession and a free press, which spread power and create spaces for independent judgement.

questions.q: Explain Marilyn Frye's birdcage metaphor and why it supports a structural understanding of oppression.
markScheme: Looking at one wire of a cage cannot explain why the bird is trapped
Only seeing the network of wires reveals the confinement
Individual barriers (e.g. dress norms, wage gaps, safety concerns) may seem trivial or justifiable alone
So oppression is a systematic network of related barriers affecting a group, not reducible to individual acts or intentions; links to Young's account
questions.modelAnswer: Frye argued that if you examine one wire of a birdcage closely, you cannot see why the bird does not simply fly round it. Only by stepping back and seeing how the wires are arranged together does the confinement become obvious. Oppression works similarly: a dress code, an expectation of childcare, a fear of walking home at night or a pay gap may each look minor or defensible when considered alone. Together they form a system that restricts a group's options in every direction. This supports a structural understanding because it locates oppression in the network of barriers rather than in any one bad actor, a view shared by Young's claim that oppression need not have an identifiable oppressor.

questions.q: Scenario: A city introduces a 'citizens' assembly' of 100 randomly selected residents to decide how to spend £10 million on regeneration. After expert presentations and three weekends of deliberation, the assembly votes to fund a new tech hub. Afterwards, researchers note that although participants mirrored the city's demographics, those with university degrees spoke for 70% of the time, and several members from a large migrant community said they felt their concerns about housing were 'not the kind of argument that counted'. Assess the assembly's democratic legitimacy using deliberative democracy and its critics.
markScheme: Explains deliberative democracy: legitimacy from free and equal public reasoning (Habermas, Cohen)
Notes strengths: random selection gives descriptive representativeness; informed deliberation; transforms preferences
Applies the 70% speaking-time data as evidence of unequal deliberative influence
Uses Young's critique: norms of 'reasonable', dispassionate argument privilege dominant groups; internal exclusion
Considers alternatives Young proposes: greeting, rhetoric, narrative
Contrast with aggregative/competitive models (Schumpeter) and accountability issues: who authorised the assembly?
Proposes remedies (facilitation, caucusing, narrative evidence)
Reasoned judgement on legitimacy
Structured, applied answer
questions.modelAnswer:
Deliberative democrats such as Habermas and Joshua Cohen hold that political decisions are legitimate when they result from free and equal citizens reasoning together, so that outcomes rest on the force of the better argument rather than on power or numbers. The assembly has real strengths on this view. Random selection produced a body that mirrored the city, avoiding the skew of self-selecting participation, and three weekends of expert input and discussion allowed considered rather than snap judgements.

The data, however, point to inequality inside the room. Participants were equal in number but not in voice: graduates took 70% of the speaking time. Iris Marion Young called this internal exclusion. People may be formally included yet find that the accepted norms of discussion, dispassionate, abstract, articulate argument, favour those already advantaged by education and class. The migrant members' sense that housing concerns were 'not the kind of argument that counted' suggests that narratives of lived experience were discounted relative to economic projections. The outcome, a tech hub rather than housing, may reflect this.

Young proposed broadening deliberation to include greeting, rhetoric and storytelling as legitimate modes of political communication. Practically, skilled facilitation, small-group work, and treating testimony as evidence could reduce the imbalance.

There are also questions from outside the deliberative model. A Schumpeterian would ask how the assembly can be held to account, since its members were not elected and cannot be removed. Defenders reply that sortition represents citizens in a different way, as a mini-public, and that final decisions can be ratified by elected councillors.

Overall, the assembly has partial legitimacy. Its selection method and deliberative structure are stronger than many conventional processes, but evidence of unequal influence undermines the claim that the result reflects free and equal reasoning. Legitimacy would be strengthened by reforms to the deliberative process rather than by abandoning deliberation.

questions.q: 'Democracy cannot be a remedy for oppression, because the oppressed are by definition a minority.' Discuss.
markScheme: Clarifies the proposition and challenges its premise: many oppressed groups are majorities (women; colonised peoples; workers; Black majorities under apartheid)
Uses Young's account: oppression is structural, not numerical
Tocqueville and Madison on majority tyranny as support for the proposition
Considers how formally democratic systems have entrenched oppression (Jim Crow; disenfranchisement)
Considers democratic responses: rights, constitutionalism, group representation (Young), deliberation
Considers Lukes/Gramsci: majorities can consent to their own subordination
Considers historical evidence that democratic movements (suffrage, civil rights, anti-colonial movements) were central to resisting oppression
Considers Anderson's point about private government: democracy confined to the state leaves workplace domination untouched
Reaches a reasoned conclusion
Clear structure
questions.modelAnswer:
The proposition rests on a premise that is false as a general matter. Oppression, on Young's account, is structural and concerns how institutions and norms disadvantage groups; it is not defined by numbers. Women are a majority in most societies, workers outnumber employers, and colonial and apartheid regimes oppressed majorities. In many cases, oppression has depended precisely on denying the majority democratic power.

There is nonetheless a truth in the claim. Where oppressed groups are minorities, majority rule can reinforce their position. Tocqueville feared majority tyranny, and Madison defended the large federal republic of the US Constitution as a way of breaking up majority factions. Jim Crow segregation was sustained by electoral majorities in Southern states, alongside the disenfranchisement of Black voters.

Even where the oppressed are numerous, democracy may fail them. Gramsci's hegemony and Lukes's third dimension explain how majorities can come to accept arrangements against their interests. Anderson's argument about private government adds that a society can be democratic in its state but authoritarian in its workplaces, where much domination occurs.

Yet the historical record shows democracy as central to remedying oppression. Women's suffrage, the US civil rights movement's campaign for voting rights culminating in the Voting Rights Act of 1965, and anti-colonial movements all demanded democratic inclusion as a means to end domination. The vote is not sufficient, but it gives a lever.

Democratic theory has also adapted. Constitutional rights and judicial review protect minorities against majorities. Young proposed group representation to ensure oppressed groups' perspectives are heard. Deliberative democrats argue that decisions must be justifiable to all, not just supported by most.

The proposition therefore fails. Democracy is not by itself a guarantee against oppression, especially of minorities, and it must be combined with rights and attention to structural power. But it has been among the most important tools by which oppressed groups, minority and majority, have resisted domination.

questions.q: 'Any theory of oppression that focuses on a single axis, whether class, race or gender, will misdescribe the experience of those it claims to liberate.' Evaluate this claim with reference to intersectionality and at least one single-axis theory.
markScheme: Defines intersectionality (Crenshaw 1989) and the legal example of Black women falling between race and sex discrimination claims
Traces earlier roots: Combahee River Collective; Anna Julia Cooper; Davis's Women, Race and Class
Sets out a single-axis theory accurately, e.g. orthodox Marxism (class primary) or early liberal/radical feminism
Gives the strongest defence of single-axis theory: explanatory parsimony, a common basis for solidarity, causal primacy claims
Considers criticisms of intersectionality: risk of infinite fragmentation, additive vs interactive models, lack of causal theory
Considers whether single-axis theories can incorporate interaction (e.g. Marxist feminism, social reproduction theory)
Distinguishes describing experience from explaining causes
Reaches a nuanced judgement
Sophisticated structure and precise use of sources
questions.modelAnswer:
The claim restates the core insight of intersectionality. Kimberlé Crenshaw (1989) showed that US courts treated discrimination claims as either race or sex claims, so Black women who faced discrimination as Black women could fall through the gap: an employer who hired white women and Black men could defend itself on both counts. More broadly, experiences of oppression are not the sum of separate axes but are shaped by their interaction. The idea has deep roots: Anna Julia Cooper insisted in 1892 that Black women's position was distinctive, the Combahee River Collective (1977) described interlocking systems, and Angela Davis's Women, Race and Class (1981) showed that the suffrage movement's racism and its neglect of working-class women followed from single-axis thinking.

A single-axis theory such as orthodox Marxism treats class as the fundamental relation, with racial and gender oppression either derived from it or secondary. Its strongest defence is explanatory. Marxists argue that capitalism's need for cheap labour and divided workforces explains why racism and sexism take the forms they do, and that class offers a basis for broad solidarity. A theory that only multiplies categories may describe experience richly while explaining little.

This points to a real weakness in some versions of intersectionality. If every combination of identities is a distinct position, it is unclear where analysis stops, and an additive model, counting disadvantages, misses the point that categories transform each other. Intersectionality is often better understood as a methodological warning than as a complete causal theory.

Single-axis theories have also evolved. Davis herself combined Marxism with analysis of race and gender, and social reproduction feminists argue that capitalism depends on unpaid, gendered and racialised care work. These are not single-axis in the crude sense.

The claim is therefore right in a precise sense: a theory that analyses only one axis will misdescribe the experiences of people at intersections, often the most marginalised. But it does not follow that we must abandon theories that give causal weight to one structure. The best position combines intersectional description with causal accounts of how class, race and gender systems interact.

questions.q: According to Rawls's difference principle, social and economic inequalities are just only if they:
options: Benefit the least advantaged members of society the most
Are deserved by those who receive them
questions.why: The difference principle permits inequalities only if they are to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged. Voluntary exchange is Nozick's test, and maximising total utility is the utilitarian one.

questions.q: Ali and Ben have equal talents and resources. Ali invests in a risky business and loses everything; Ben is blinded in an accident he could not have foreseen. For a luck egalitarian like Dworkin, which is correct?
options: Neither should be compensated, since both outcomes resulted from life in a free society
Ben's loss is brute luck and calls for compensation; Ali's loss is option luck and need not
Ali's loss is brute luck since he could not foresee the market
questions.why: Dworkin distinguishes option luck (outcomes of deliberate, calculated gambles) from brute luck (risks not deliberately taken). Equality of resources should neutralise brute luck but let option luck stand, subject to insurance.

questions.q: Nozick's Wilt Chamberlain example is mainly intended to show that:
options: Patterned principles of justice can be maintained only by continually interfering with people's liberty
Taxation is justified to fund public goods
questions.why: Free transfers upset any starting pattern, so maintaining the pattern requires interfering with voluntary exchanges. Nozick does not argue from desert or efficiency.

questions.q: Explain why Rawls thought parties in the original position would choose his two principles rather than utilitarianism.
markScheme: Behind the veil of ignorance, parties do not know their place in society, talents or conception of the good
High stakes and a one-off choice with no probabilities make maximin reasoning rational
Utilitarianism could permit sacrificing some (even their basic liberties) for greater aggregate welfare, which parties could not accept if they turned out to be the losers
The strains of commitment and the need for a stable, publicly justifiable agreement favour the two principles; utilitarianism ignores the separateness of persons
questions.modelAnswer: In the original position, parties choose principles behind a veil of ignorance about their class, talents, sex and conception of the good. Rawls argued that because the choice is one-off, the stakes are fundamental, and the parties lack reliable probabilities, they would reason by maximin, securing the best worst outcome. Utilitarianism might sacrifice the interests or even the liberties of some for a larger total, which would be disastrous for anyone who ended up in that position. They would also consider the strains of commitment: they could not in good faith agree to principles they might be unable to live with. Rawls summarised this by saying utilitarianism does not take seriously the separateness of persons.

questions.q: Outline Elizabeth Anderson's critique of luck egalitarianism and her alternative of democratic equality.
markScheme: Luck egalitarianism aims to neutralise unchosen disadvantage while holding people responsible for choices
Harshness objection: it abandons the imprudent, e.g. an uninsured negligent driver
Disrespect objection: compensating people for inferior talents expresses contempt and requires intrusive judgements
Democratic (relational) equality: the aim is to end oppression and secure standing as equals in society
Guarantees capabilities needed to function as an equal citizen, regardless of fault
questions.modelAnswer: Luck egalitarians hold that inequalities from unchosen circumstances should be eliminated while those from choices can stand. Anderson's 'What Is the Point of Equality?' (1999) argued this is mistaken in two ways. It is harsh, because it can leave the imprudent, such as an uninsured driver who causes an accident, without help. It is also disrespectful, since compensating people for being untalented requires the state to judge them inferior. Anderson's alternative, democratic equality, says the point of equality is to end oppression and create a community in which people stand as equals. The state should guarantee everyone the capabilities needed to function as an equal citizen, regardless of whether their disadvantage was their fault.

questions.q: Scenario: Arkland has two policy options. Under Policy X, the poorest 20% have an average income of £12,000 and the richest 20% have £60,000. Under Policy Y, a tax cut stimulates growth: the poorest 20% have £13,000 and the richest 20% have £110,000. Policy Y is funded by reducing state school spending, which data suggest will lower the chances of children from poor families entering professional jobs. Which policy would (i) Rawls, (ii) Nozick and (iii) a strict egalitarian prefer? Explain your reasoning and give your own assessment.
markScheme: Correctly computes and notes ratio change: X is 5:1, Y is about 8.5:1; poorest gain £1,000 under Y
Difference principle alone appears to favour Y, since the least advantaged are better off
But Rawls's fair equality of opportunity has lexical priority over the difference principle; cuts to schooling that reduce poor children's chances violate it, so Rawls would likely reject Y
Nozick judges by process, not outcomes: tax cuts reduce redistributive taking; but he would not support state schooling as a matter of justice; likely favours Y or is indifferent to the pattern
Strict egalitarian prefers X as more equal; levelling-down objection if equality is valued intrinsically
Prioritarian/sufficientarian alternatives mentioned
Own assessment, with reasoning
Clear structure; accurate use of numbers
questions.modelAnswer:
Under Policy X the top quintile has five times the income of the bottom; under Y the ratio rises to about 8.5 to 1, but the bottom quintile gains £1,000.

Rawls's difference principle, read in isolation, seems to favour Y, because inequality is permitted when it improves the position of the least advantaged, and here it does. But Rawls's principles are lexically ordered: fair equality of opportunity takes priority over the difference principle. People with similar talents and willingness to use them should have similar prospects regardless of class. Cutting state school spending in a way that reduces poor children's chances of entering professional jobs violates this principle, so a gain in income cannot compensate for it. Rawls would therefore probably reject Y, or require it to be funded differently.

Nozick evaluates distributions by their history, not their pattern. A tax cut reduces what he regarded as taking the fruits of people's labour, so he would welcome it. He would not regard state school spending as required by justice, though he would not object to private charity. The widening ratio is irrelevant to him; what matters is whether holdings arose from just acquisition and transfer.

A strict egalitarian prefers X because it is more equal. But Y makes the poor better off, so preferring X involves accepting that the poor have less for the sake of equality. This is the levelling-down objection. A prioritarian would avoid it by giving extra weight to gains for the worst off, which here favour Y on income, though the educational effects would also count.

My own view is that Rawls offers the most persuasive analysis. The income gain to the poor matters, which counts against strict egalitarianism, but income is not the only good; opportunity and the social bases of self-respect matter too. Policy Y is objectionable less for its inequality than for entrenching class disadvantage across generations. A version of Y funded without education cuts would be defensible on Rawlsian grounds.

questions.q: 'Taxation of earnings from labour is on a par with forced labour' (Nozick). Discuss.
markScheme: Explains the claim and its basis in self-ownership and the entitlement theory
Explains the reasoning: taking n hours' earnings is like forcing n hours' work for another's purposes
Considers disanalogies: taxed person chooses whether and how much to work; no one directs their labour
Considers the objection that property rights are conventional and defined by law, so pre-tax income is not naturally one's own (Murphy and Nagel, 'myth of ownership')
Considers Locke's proviso and whether historical acquisition was just; rectification would itself require redistribution
Considers Rawls: talents are morally arbitrary, social cooperation produces earnings
Considers G. A. Cohen on self-ownership: accepting self-ownership does not settle ownership of external resources
Evaluates whether Nozick's position is internally consistent
Reaches a justified conclusion
Structured, accurate argument
questions.modelAnswer:
Nozick's claim follows from his entitlement theory. If people own themselves, they own their labour, and if they acquire holdings through just acquisition and voluntary transfer, they are entitled to them. Taxing the earnings of n hours of work takes the product of those hours for purposes the worker did not choose, which Nozick compared to forcing someone to work n hours for another. Redistributive taxation thus treats people as partly owned by others.

The analogy has notable disanalogies. A taxed worker chooses whether to work, in what job, and for how long; no one directs their activity. Someone who prefers leisure can avoid income tax by working less, whereas a forced labourer cannot avoid the labour. Nozick anticipated this, arguing that people who prefer goods requiring income are treated worse than those who prefer leisure, but this seems a complaint about unequal treatment rather than about forced labour.

A deeper objection concerns the baseline. Murphy and Nagel argue that pre-tax income is not naturally one's own: property and markets are legal creations, and the tax system is part of defining what people own. On this view taxation does not take something already owned; it is part of the rules that create ownership.

Nozick's own theory also exposes him. Entitlement depends on just acquisition, and Locke's proviso requires leaving 'enough and as good' for others. Given that actual holdings result from conquest, slavery and enclosure, Nozick's principle of rectification may itself demand large-scale redistribution. Rawls adds that natural talents and the social cooperation that makes them valuable are not deserved, so earnings are not simply the product of individual effort.

G. A. Cohen made a further point: even granting self-ownership, it does not follow that people may appropriate unequal shares of external resources. Self-ownership is compatible with joint ownership of the world.

Nozick's claim is therefore rhetorically powerful but philosophically weak. Taxation does involve coercion and needs justification, but the comparison with forced labour depends on a contested natural-property baseline and ignores the social conditions that make earnings possible.

questions.q: 'Egalitarians should stop worrying about how much people have and start worrying about how they relate to one another.' Evaluate this claim.
markScheme: Distinguishes distributive egalitarianism (Rawls, Dworkin, luck egalitarianism) from relational egalitarianism (Anderson, Scheffler, Young)
Explains the relational critique: the point of equality is to end oppression and hierarchy, not to distribute goods according to luck
Considers the harshness and disrespect objections to luck egalitarianism
Considers whether relational equality nonetheless has distributive implications (sufficiency of capabilities, limits on inequality that converts to domination)
Considers objections to relational egalitarianism: vagueness, indeterminacy, whether it can explain global or intergenerational justice where there is no relationship
Considers prioritarianism, sufficientarianism and levelling down
Considers Rawls as combining both (social bases of self-respect; fair value of political liberties)
Uses examples (e.g. wealth enabling political capture; poverty creating dependency) to show interaction
Reaches a clear, nuanced conclusion
Sophisticated, well-organised argument
questions.modelAnswer:
The claim reflects a debate between distributive and relational egalitarians. Distributive egalitarians ask what goods people should have: resources for Dworkin, primary goods for Rawls, or compensation for brute bad luck for luck egalitarians. Relational egalitarians, notably Elizabeth Anderson and Samuel Scheffler, argue that the point of equality is to create a society in which people relate as equals, without domination, exploitation, marginalisation or stigma.

The relational critique has force. Anderson showed that luck egalitarianism can be harsh, abandoning those whose disadvantage results from imprudence, and disrespectful, requiring officials to certify people as untalented or unlucky in order to compensate them. It also seems to locate injustice in nature rather than in social relations. Historically, egalitarian movements, against caste, slavery, patriarchy and aristocracy, were struggles against hierarchy rather than for equal shares of a pie. Young's critique of the distributive paradigm makes a similar point: oppression involves decision-making power, division of labour and culture, not only goods.

However, the claim's either/or framing is misleading. Relational equality has distributive implications. Anderson's own view requires guaranteeing the capabilities needed to function as an equal citizen, which demands resources. Large inequalities of wealth can convert into domination: the rich can capture politics, and the poor depend on employers and landlords. Rawls recognised this in insisting on the fair value of political liberties and the social bases of self-respect. So caring about relations requires caring about distribution.

Relational theories also face challenges. 'Relating as equals' can be vague, offering little guidance on how much inequality is too much. It is unclear how they address injustice between people who do not interact, such as distant strangers or future generations, where distributive duties like Singer's seem more natural.

The best view is that relational equality supplies the point of equality while distribution supplies much of its content. Egalitarians should not stop worrying about how much people have; they should worry about it because, and largely to the extent that, it shapes whether people can stand as equals. This avoids the levelling-down objection, explains why poverty and extreme wealth both matter, and keeps justice tied to real social relations.

questions.q: In Leviathan, Hobbes describes life in the state of nature as:
options: Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short
Free, equal and governed by natural law that all obey
questions.why: This is Hobbes's famous description in chapter 13. The 'inconvenient' state of nature is Locke's, and natural compassion is Rousseau's.

questions.q: Which statement best captures Hayek's objection to the idea of 'social justice'?
options: Market outcomes are just because people deserve what they earn
Justice applies only to the intended actions of agents, and market distributions are not intended by anyone
Inequality is necessary to motivate effort, so it is always just
Redistribution is wrong because it violates natural rights of self-ownership
questions.why: Hayek argued that calling an unintended market outcome unjust is a category mistake. He explicitly denied that market rewards track desert, and the self-ownership argument is Nozick's.

questions.q: Identify Marx's four aspects of alienated labour in the 1844 Manuscripts.
markScheme: Alienation from the product of labour, which belongs to another and confronts the worker as an alien power
Alienation from the activity of labour, which is forced and not an expression of the worker's own will
Alienation from species-being, the distinctively human capacity for free, conscious, creative activity
Alienation from other people, since relations are mediated by competition and the market
questions.modelAnswer: In the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, Marx argued that under capitalism the worker is alienated in four related ways. First, from the product, which belongs to the capitalist and stands over the worker as an alien power. Second, from the activity of labour, which is coerced and experienced as a means to survival rather than self-expression. Third, from species-being: humans are distinguished by free, conscious, creative production, but wage labour reduces this to a mere means of existence. Fourth, from other people, since relations between workers and with capitalists are shaped by competition and exchange rather than mutual recognition.

questions.q: Compare Hobbes's and Rousseau's accounts of the state of nature.
markScheme: Hobbes: war of all against all, driven by competition, diffidence and glory under rough equality and scarcity
Rousseau: natural humans are solitary, largely peaceful, guided by amour de soi and pity (compassion)
Rousseau accused Hobbes of attributing to natural man passions such as pride that are products of society (amour-propre)

Different implications: Hobbes argues for absolute sovereignty to escape war; Rousseau argues that inequality and conflict are social, so a legitimate association must transform rather than merely restrain humanity
questions.modelAnswer: For Hobbes, people in the state of nature are roughly equal and face scarcity, so competition, distrust and the desire for glory produce a war of every one against every one. Rational fear drives them to institute an absolute sovereign. Rousseau, in the Discourse on Inequality, objected that Hobbes had read social vices back into nature. Natural humans were solitary, with few needs, moved by healthy self-love (amour de soi) and pity, and so largely peaceful. Conflict comes from society, property and amour-propre, the desire for others' esteem. Hence Rousseau's solution is not a sovereign to restrain naturally dangerous people but a just association, governed by the general will, that reshapes social relations.

questions.q: Hobbes and Hayek both defend strong limits on popular political action, yet for opposite reasons. Explain and assess this claim.
markScheme: Hobbes: fear of disorder; undivided, absolute sovereign needed; division of sovereignty or popular resistance leads to civil war
Hayek: fear of concentrated, unlimited government power, including democratic majorities; supports rule of law and constitutional limits
Hobbes concentrates power to secure peace; Hayek disperses or limits power to protect liberty and spontaneous order
Both distrust collective will as a guide (Hobbes: private judgement causes conflict; Hayek: no one has the knowledge to direct society)
Assessment: the 'opposite reasons' framing is partly right but both share an epistemic or anti-rationalist distrust of collective purposes
Clear concluding judgement
questions.modelAnswer: Hobbes limits popular action by concentrating authority: because private judgements of right conflict, subjects must authorise an undivided sovereign whose decisions are final, since divided sovereignty or resistance on grounds of conscience risks civil war. Hayek limits it by restricting government: even democratic majorities must be bound by general rules, because unlimited power invites coercion and no authority commands the dispersed knowledge needed to direct society. One concentrates power to secure peace; the other constrains it to protect liberty and spontaneous order. Yet both distrust a collective will pursuing substantive shared ends, Hobbes because judgements diverge, Hayek because knowledge is dispersed. The claim captures their institutional conclusions but understates this shared scepticism.

questions.q: Scenario: After a decade of civil war, the country of Lothar holds a constitutional convention. Delegate A proposes an all-powerful executive with no judicial review, arguing that only undivided authority can prevent renewed conflict. Delegate B proposes direct citizen assemblies for all legislation, rejecting elected representatives. Delegate C proposes a central planning board to rebuild the economy rapidly. Delegate D proposes strict constitutional limits on government economic intervention and a guaranteed minimum income. Identify which of Hobbes, Rousseau, Marx and Hayek each proposal most closely reflects, and assess which combination would best secure a legitimate and stable order.
markScheme: A = Hobbes: absolute, undivided sovereignty to escape the state of nature; rights of self-preservation remain
B = Rousseau: sovereignty cannot be represented; general will expressed by assembled citizens; feasibility concerns (Rousseau himself thought it suited small states)
C = Marx (or Marxist tradition): collective control of production; note Marx himself wrote little on detailed planning
D = Hayek: rule of law, limits on discretion, knowledge problem; he accepted a guaranteed minimum outside the market
Applies each to post-war context: security, legitimacy, economic reconstruction
Evaluates tensions, e.g. Hobbes's security vs Rousseau's participation; Hayek's knowledge problem vs Marx's critique of market exploitation
Considers legitimacy in terms of consent/participation and stability
Argued conclusion on best combination
Clear structure
questions.modelAnswer:
Delegate A echoes Hobbes. After civil war, Hobbes's case is at its strongest: without a common power to keep all in awe, people revert to fear and pre-emptive violence, and dividing sovereignty, for instance between executive and courts, invites rival claims to final authority. Even Hobbes allowed subjects to resist threats to their lives, though, and an unchecked executive in a post-conflict state could itself become the threat.

Delegate B reflects Rousseau, who held that sovereignty, the exercise of the general will, cannot be represented and must be exercised by citizens directly. This promises strong legitimacy, since citizens obey laws they make. But Rousseau himself thought such republics suited small states with relatively equal citizens, and in a divided post-war society assemblies may reproduce factional conflict rather than produce a general will.

Delegate C draws on the Marxist tradition of collective control of production, aimed at ending exploitation and the class divisions that may have fuelled the war. Marx himself said little about how planning would work, and Hayek's objection applies: a planning board cannot gather the dispersed, local knowledge that prices transmit, and concentrating economic power in an unaccountable body is dangerous.

Delegate D is Hayekian: general rules limiting discretionary intervention protect liberty and allow spontaneous order, while a guaranteed minimum, which Hayek did accept, provides security without central direction.

The best combination takes from each. Hobbes's insight that peace requires an effective, unified authority supports a strong state capable of disarming factions, but legitimacy and long-term stability require accountability, which Hobbes neglects. Rousseau's concern for participation suggests mechanisms such as referendums or local assemblies alongside representation. Hayek's knowledge problem counts against comprehensive planning, but Marx's concern about inequality supports a guaranteed minimum and broad access to the economy. Stability rests on both security and the belief that the order is the citizens' own.

questions.q: 'Rousseau's general will is either empty or tyrannical.' Discuss.
markScheme: Accurate account of the general will: aims at the common good of citizens as citizens; distinct from the will of all; inalienable and indivisible sovereignty
'Empty' horn: if the general will is just whatever the common good is, it gives no procedure for identifying it; the will of all may diverge; role of the Legislator
'Tyrannical' horn: 'forced to be free'; civil religion; Berlin and Talmon's reading
Considers Rousseau's conditions: laws must be general in form and object; citizens vote on what the general will is; no partial associations; rough equality
Democratic or procedural interpretations (e.g. citizens deliberating as citizens); Condorcet jury theorem readings
Considers republican readings: freedom as not being dependent on any particular will
Evaluates whether 'forced to be free' can be read as protection against personal dependence
Reaches a reasoned conclusion
Coherent structure
questions.modelAnswer:
Rousseau's general will is the will of citizens directed at their common good as members of the political community, as opposed to the will of all, which is just the sum of private interests. Sovereignty consists in exercising the general will, and it cannot be alienated or represented. The dilemma is that the concept seems either to give no guidance or to license oppression.

The 'empty' horn arises because Rousseau admits the people can be deceived and that the will of all may differ from the general will. If the general will is defined by the common good, then knowing what it is requires knowing the common good independently, and voting becomes at best evidence. Rousseau's introduction of a quasi-divine Legislator to shape the people suggests he doubted ordinary citizens could find it unaided.

The 'tyrannical' horn arises from his claim that whoever refuses to obey the general will shall be forced to be free, and from his civil religion, which allowed banishment of those who rejected its dogmas. Berlin and J. L. Talmon read Rousseau as an ancestor of totalitarian democracy, in which the state claims to embody citizens' real will.

Both horns can be blunted. Rousseau gave the general will formal constraints: laws must be general, applying equally to all and not singling out individuals. Citizens are asked not what they want but what the general will is, which turns voting into a process of public judgement, a reading that links Rousseau to deliberative democracy and, some argue, to Condorcet's jury theorem. Factions and great inequalities are to be avoided precisely because they corrupt this judgement.

On a republican reading, 'forced to be free' means that the law protects each citizen against personal dependence on any other individual. Being compelled to obey general laws one shares in making is freedom compared with being at the mercy of private wills.

The dilemma is therefore false, though it identifies genuine tensions. The general will is not empty, because generality and equality constrain it, and it is not inherently tyrannical. But it is fragile: its benign form depends on demanding social conditions, and where those are absent the language of the general will can be exploited to silence dissent.

questions.q: 'Marx and Hayek agree on more than either would admit: both see the market as an impersonal order beyond any individual's control.' Critically evaluate this claim.
markScheme: Explains Hayek's view: market as spontaneous order (cosmos); prices coordinate dispersed knowledge; outcomes unintended; this is a virtue
Explains Marx's view: under capitalism social relations appear as relations between things (commodity fetishism); market forces dominate producers; impersonal domination
Identifies genuine agreement: both see market outcomes as unintended and not under conscious control
Key disagreement: Hayek sees impersonality as protecting freedom from arbitrary will; Marx sees it as alienation and domination
Disagreement over knowledge: Hayek says no one can master the social order; Marx anticipates conscious collective control by associated producers
Disagreement over exploitation and class: Marx locates domination in the wage relation; Hayek sees voluntary exchange
Assesses who has the better of the debate, e.g. Hayek's knowledge problem against planning, Marx's critique of formally free but compelled labour
Considers whether impersonal domination can be non-arbitrary (link to republicanism)
Reaches a nuanced, justified conclusion
Sophisticated structure
questions.modelAnswer:
There is a striking overlap. Hayek argued that the market is a spontaneous order, the result of human action but not of human design. Prices transmit dispersed, often tacit knowledge that no planner could gather, and the resulting distribution is intended by no one. Marx also emphasised that under capitalism social relations escape the control of those who create them. In his analysis of commodity fetishism in Capital, relations between people appear as relations between things, and producers are governed by market movements they collectively cause but individually cannot resist. Both, then, see the market as an impersonal order beyond any individual's control.

The agreement stops at description. For Hayek impersonality is a virtue. Because no one designs market outcomes, no one is subjected to another's arbitrary will, and it is a category mistake to call outcomes unjust. Impersonal rules protect liberty. For Marx impersonality is itself a form of domination. Workers lacking means of production are compelled to sell their labour power, and capitalists too must accumulate or perish. People are ruled by abstractions of their own making, a form of alienation.

They also disagree about whether the order can be mastered. Hayek thought the knowledge problem made rational central direction impossible. Marx anticipated a society of associated producers who would bring production under conscious collective control. On this point the twentieth-century experience of planned economies gives Hayek considerable support, though Marx said little about planning's mechanics.

On exploitation and class, however, Marx has a stronger case. Hayek treats exchange as voluntary, but the formal freedom of the wage contract coexists with structural compulsion. Republican theorists add that impersonal forces can produce dependence on particular employers or landlords who wield arbitrary power, which Hayek's focus on the state neglects.

The claim is thus partly correct. Marx and Hayek share an analysis of the market as an unplanned order that no individual controls, and this unites them against naive views of markets as simple aggregations of choices. But they evaluate this fact in opposite ways, and that evaluative disagreement, over whether impersonal compulsion is freedom or domination, is the heart of the matter rather than a detail.

questions.q: Kwame Nkrumah led which country to independence in 1957?
questions.why: Nkrumah led the Gold Coast to independence as Ghana on 6 March 1957, usually described as the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence from European rule.

questions.q: Which work by Angela Davis argues for prison abolition and analyses the 'prison-industrial complex'?
options: Neo-Colonialism: The Last Stage of Imperialism
questions.why: Are Prisons Obsolete? (2003) is Davis's abolitionist text. Women, Race and Class is also hers but addresses race, class and the women's movement; the other two are by Cooper and Nkrumah.

questions.q: Summarise the central argument of Frederick Douglass's speech 'What to the Slave is the Fourth of July?' (1852).
markScheme: Delivered on 5 July 1852 in Rochester to an audience celebrating American independence
Argues that the celebration of liberty is, to the enslaved, a mockery that reveals national hypocrisy

Contrasts the founders' principles of liberty with the practice of slavery, appealing to those principles (and, later in the speech, the Constitution, which he called a 'glorious liberty document') against slavery
questions.modelAnswer: In his Rochester speech of 5 July 1852, Douglass praised the founders' principles of liberty but asked what the Fourth of July meant to the enslaved. His answer was that it revealed the gross injustice to which they were subject: the nation's celebration of freedom was, to them, a sham and a mockery. By measuring American practice against America's own professed ideals, Douglass exposed its hypocrisy, while also expressing hope that those ideals, including the Constitution, which he argued was not pro-slavery, could be turned against slavery.

questions.q: Explain Nkrumah's concept of neo-colonialism and assess its relevance to debates about legitimacy and sovereignty.
markScheme: Neo-colonialism: a state is formally independent with the outward trappings of sovereignty, but its economic system and hence its policy are directed from outside
Mechanisms: foreign control of investment, trade, aid, finance and resources; title echoes Lenin's Imperialism
Implication for legitimacy: formal self-determination may mask continuing domination; consent of the governed is undermined if real decisions lie elsewhere
Assessment point, e.g. supports structural accounts of power; critics argue it can be used to deflect responsibility from domestic elites, including Nkrumah's own authoritarianism
questions.modelAnswer: In Neo-Colonialism: The Last Stage of Imperialism (1965), Nkrumah argued that a state can be formally independent, with a flag, seat at the UN and the trappings of sovereignty, while its economy, and therefore its policy, is directed from outside through foreign investment, debt, aid conditions and control of commodity prices. This matters for legitimacy because popular sovereignty means little if key decisions are effectively made elsewhere, so formal independence can mask continuing domination. The concept parallels Lindblom's structural power of capital at an international level. Critics note that it can be used to deflect attention from domestic failures; Nkrumah's own government became a one-party state before his overthrow in 1966.

questions.q: How does Anna Julia Cooper's A Voice from the South (1892) anticipate later debates about intersectionality?
markScheme: Cooper argued Black women's position was distinctive, facing both a 'woman question' and a 'race problem'
She criticised racism among white feminists and sexism among Black male leaders
'When and where I enter' claim: Black women's advancement is the measure of the race's progress
Anticipates Crenshaw and the Combahee River Collective in treating race and gender as interacting, not separable
Evaluative point: differences from later intersectional theory, e.g. Cooper's emphasis on education, respectability and Christian ideals; less attention to class
questions.modelAnswer: Cooper argued that Black women faced both a woman question and a race problem, and criticised white feminists who excluded them and Black male leaders who neglected women's education. Her claim that only the Black woman can say 'when and where I enter' the whole race enters with her makes Black women's position the test of racial progress. This anticipates Crenshaw's insight that discrimination at the intersection is not the sum of separate forms. Cooper's framework differs, though: it is grounded in Christian and classical ideals and gives less attention to class and economic structure than later Black feminist thought such as Davis's.

questions.q: Scenario: A university's politics department is reviewing its first-year reading list, which currently includes Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Mill, Marx and Rawls. A proposal suggests adding Douglass, Cooper, Nkrumah and Davis. One academic objects: 'These are activists and politicians, not systematic philosophers; they belong on a history or sociology course.' Another replies that 'the canon reflects who had power to write and be read, not who had the best ideas.' Evaluate both positions, using at least two of the four thinkers to show what their work contributes to political theory.
markScheme: States the objection: canonical status is about systematic argument; activists' writings are context-bound
Notes that canonical thinkers were also political actors (Locke, Marx, Mill as MP), weakening the distinction
Douglass: theory of freedom from the standpoint of the enslaved; critique of national hypocrisy; argument about the Constitution
Cooper: early analysis of interlocking race and gender oppression
Nkrumah: neo-colonialism as structural domination; legitimacy and sovereignty
Davis: abolition, prison-industrial complex; analysis of race, class and gender
Evaluates the second position: exclusion reflects power (link to Mills, Pateman, Lukes); but also needs a standard for inclusion
Considers whether inclusion should be on grounds of argument quality, perspective or historical significance
Reasoned conclusion
Clear structure
questions.modelAnswer:
The first academic's objection assumes a sharp line between systematic philosophy and political writing. The line is hard to hold. Locke wrote the Second Treatise amid the political crises of the 1680s, Marx was an organiser and journalist, and Mill was an MP. Canonical texts are frequently interventions in political struggles. What matters is whether a work contains arguments that illuminate core concepts such as freedom, power and legitimacy.

On that test the proposed thinkers qualify. Douglass analyses freedom from the standpoint of those denied it. His Narrative presents literacy and resistance as the routes from slavery to selfhood, and his 1852 speech exposes the gap between liberal principles and practice, a theme that anticipates Charles Mills's racial contract. His shift towards reading the Constitution as anti-slavery engages directly with questions of legitimacy and political obligation.

Nkrumah's account of neo-colonialism offers a theory of structural domination: formal sovereignty can coexist with external control of a state's economy. This complements Lukes and Lindblom on power and challenges legitimacy theories that equate independence with self-government.

Cooper and Davis contribute analyses of interlocking oppressions. Cooper's A Voice from the South argued in 1892 that Black women's position revealed what both race and gender politics missed; Davis's work on race, class and prisons develops this with Marxist tools and raises questions about punishment and state power that canonical theory often ignores.

The second academic's claim has force. Canons reflect who had access to education, publishers and universities, and Pateman and Mills show how exclusion shaped the content of theory, not just its authorship. But the claim alone is not enough: an inclusive curriculum still needs criteria, or it becomes a list of identities rather than arguments.

The best position is that these thinkers should be included because their arguments are illuminating, and those arguments were overlooked partly because of who made them. Teaching them alongside Hobbes and Rawls, in dialogue on freedom and legitimacy, strengthens both.

questions.q: 'Freedom means nothing unless it is defined by those who have been denied it.' Discuss with reference to Douglass and at least one of Cooper, Nkrumah or Davis.
markScheme: Interprets the proposition: a standpoint claim about who has epistemic authority over the meaning of freedom
Douglass: freedom as more than legal status; literacy, self-assertion (Covey fight), exposure of hypocrisy
Relates Douglass to republican non-domination: the kind master problem
Nkrumah: political independence vs freedom from neo-colonial domination
Davis: freedom beyond formal emancipation; continuity of slavery, convict leasing, incarceration; abolition democracy
Cooper: freedom requires recognition of Black women's distinctive position and access to higher education
Evaluates standpoint epistemology: insight from experience vs risk of relativism or essentialism; the oppressed do not speak with one voice
Compares with canonical theorists (Berlin, Mill, Pettit) to show what these perspectives add or confirm
Reasoned conclusion that qualifies the strong claim
Well-organised argument
questions.modelAnswer:
The proposition makes a standpoint claim: those who have experienced unfreedom understand freedom best, so definitions offered by the free are likely to be partial. Read strongly, it says other definitions are meaningless; read weakly, it says that the perspectives of the unfree are indispensable.

Douglass supports the weak reading powerfully. His Narrative shows that freedom is not just the absence of chains. Learning to read revealed his condition to him, and his resistance to Covey restored a sense of himself as a man rather than property. His experience also clarifies a theoretical point: a kind master still holds arbitrary power, so enslavement is defined by dependence rather than by the frequency of interference. This is precisely the republican conception later developed by Pettit and Skinner, and it shows how theories built on the standpoint of the enslaved expose limits in Berlin's non-interference model.

Nkrumah extends this to nations. Political independence, which he once treated as the 'political kingdom' to be sought first, proved insufficient where economies remained externally controlled. Freedom must include freedom from neo-colonial domination, a lesson learned through Ghana's experience rather than derived abstractly.

Davis argues that formal emancipation in 1865 did not end unfreedom, since convict leasing and later mass incarceration reproduced racialised control. Drawing on Du Bois's idea of abolition democracy, she argues that freedom requires building institutions, education, health care, that make prisons unnecessary.

Yet the strong reading fails. Experience of oppression gives insight but does not settle the meaning of freedom, and the oppressed do not agree among themselves: Douglass's liberal constitutionalism differs from Davis's Marxism. Treating any group as having automatic authority risks essentialism. Moreover, Douglass appealed to principles of liberty articulated by others and turned them against slavery, which suggests freedom's meaning is contested and shared, not owned.

The proposition is best accepted in its weaker form. A theory of freedom that ignores those denied it is likely to mistake the privileges of the free for the essence of freedom. But the result is a more adequate universal concept, not a definition belonging to one group.

questions.q: 'Angela Davis's case for prison abolition shows that the liberal theory of legitimate coercion is not merely incomplete but fundamentally flawed.' Critically evaluate this claim.
markScheme: Outlines liberal theories of legitimate coercion: Weber's monopoly of legitimate force; Mill's harm principle; consent and fair play; Rawlsian punishment within a just scheme
Explains Davis's argument: prison-industrial complex, continuity from slavery and convict leasing, prisons as a way of disappearing social problems
Explains that abolition is a positive project (building alternatives), not only removal
Evaluates the 'incomplete' reading: liberals can accept critiques of racist practice and argue for reform within liberal principles
Evaluates the 'fundamentally flawed' reading: liberal theory abstracts from history and structure (link to Mills, Pateman); legitimacy of coercion depends on background justice
Considers objections to abolition: protection of victims, serious violence, need for some coercive institutions
Considers connections to Young's structural oppression, Foucault's disciplinary power or republican domination
Distinguishes critique of prisons from critique of coercion as such
Reaches a careful, justified conclusion
Sophisticated argument and accurate use of sources
questions.modelAnswer:
Liberal theories justify state coercion in various ways. Weber described the state as claiming a monopoly of legitimate force; Mill held that coercion is justified to prevent harm to others; consent and fair play theories explain why citizens must accept penalties; and Rawls treated punishment as part of a scheme of rules that would be just under fair conditions. Common to these is the idea that coercion can be legitimate if it follows justified principles and fair procedures.

Davis's Are Prisons Obsolete? (2003) challenges this at several levels. She traces continuities from slavery through post-emancipation convict leasing to mass incarceration, arguing that prisons have functioned to control racialised and poor populations. The prison-industrial complex creates economic and political interests in incarceration. Prisons also serve as a place where people treated as undesirable are deposited, relieving society of the responsibility of addressing poverty, addiction and mental illness; as Davis puts it, prisons do not disappear problems, they disappear human beings. Abolition is a positive project of building alternatives, not simply closing prisons.

One reading treats this as showing liberal theory incomplete. A liberal could accept that racist policing and sentencing violate equal treatment and that much incarceration fails the harm principle, while insisting that the principles themselves are sound. Reform, decriminalisation and restorative justice can be justified on liberal grounds.

The stronger reading says the flaw lies deeper. Liberal theories of legitimate coercion typically assume a background of rough justice and ask whether particular penalties are fair. Charles Mills and Iris Marion Young argue that this abstraction hides structural domination: if the background is unjust, punishing those it disadvantages compounds injustice rather than restoring fairness. On this view the legitimacy of punishment cannot be assessed apart from the justice of the society that punishes, and liberal theory characteristically separates them.

There are limits. Abolitionism must still say how to protect people from serious violence, and most abolitionists accept some forms of accountability. Davis's argument targets prisons as an institution rather than coercion as such, so it does not show that all legitimate coercion is impossible.

The claim is thus overstated but contains a significant truth. Davis does not refute the idea that coercion can be legitimate. She shows that liberal theory's habitual abstraction from history and structure makes it blind to how coercive institutions reproduce domination. That is more than a gap to be filled but less than a refutation; it requires liberal theory to make background justice a condition of legitimate punishment.
